Environmental Quality Sector

A7. MONITORING SYSTEM FOR WATER QUALITY IN THE TOCUYO RIVER AND TUY RIVER BASINS

Sector: Environmental Quality

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The progressive degradation of water quality in rivers and seas, caused mainly by pollution from various sources, such as industrial discharges, agricultural activities and urban waste, generates a series of negative consequences, associated with the loss of biological diversity, risks to human health, among others.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

  • Beneficiaries: Local communities that will be able to gain access to safe drinking water for human consumption, reducing the risk of water-related diseases, and farmers who will be able to use water resources in the production of healthy, quality food.
  • Users: Water resource users, MinAguas, MINEC.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Achieve the consolidation of a water quality monitoring system that makes it possible to verify the load of environmental pollutants discharged into the Tocuyo River and Tuy River basins, which are also used as drinking water supply for the main cities of Lara, Caracas and Miranda (respectively). With the system, it is expected to track environmental parameters related to climate change, making it possible to strengthen the database to build water quality indices for each of these water bodies during the period 2025-2030; detect any problem in time and take the necessary control measures.

4 | Value proposition

With the water quality monitoring system, the following is foreseen:

  • Improve water quality.
  • Increase the protection of biological diversity.
  • Reduce morbidity rates related to waterborne diseases.
  • Promote more sustainable water management, guaranteeing its quality for future generations.

5 | Adaptation options

Strengthening of the water quality monitoring systems of the Tocuyo River and the Tuy River.

6 | Key activities

  • Meetings for inter-institutional cooperation.
  • Strengthening of analytical capacities.
  • Design and execution of the environmental monitoring and analysis plan.
  • Integration of data and digital platforms.
  • Citizen participation and environmental education.
  • Continuous evaluation and improvement of the monitoring systems.
  • Strengthening of multisectoral governance.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The water quality monitoring system in the Tocuyo River and Tuy River basins is considered both a social information option and an enabling measure aimed at fostering awareness of the relationship between climate change and water quality.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

The consolidation of the monitoring system:

  • Facilitates compliance with international and national commitments on water quality.
  • Provides reliable information for the formulation and evaluation of public policies related to water.
  • Makes it possible to anticipate and respond to pollution events, minimizing negative impacts.
  • Provides high-quality data for scientific research on aquatic ecosystems and climate change.
  • Fosters specific staff training.
  • Considers the inclusion and hiring of human talent and technological resources.

A8. PREDICTION OF EMERGING ADVERSE CLIMATE SCENARIOS

Sector: Science and Technology

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

According to the most recent evidence, the speed and direction of actual and potential climate change has been underestimated by the models currently used for vulnerability assessments, as well as for identifying the best adaptation strategies.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: The beneficiary population consists of policymakers, the productive sector, the scientific community and the general population.

Users: All inhabitants of Venezuela will benefit directly and indirectly, as well as the various political, economic and/or natural, national and/or regional divisions and subdivisions that may be identified or emerge as being of special interest due to their current or future vulnerability or strategic value.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Improve the capacity to predict reliable emerging adverse scenarios and to assess the best options to help cope with the impacts generated by the current unprecedented climate dynamics, through the application of models that include in their simulations historically underestimated environmental variables (for example, oceanic variables), with a proven capacity to establish important teleconnections with the actual and potential climate dynamics of Venezuela and the region.

4 | Value proposition

Generate reliable and timely information to identify Climate Change scenarios with the actual and potential capacity to directly affect, through complex and even distant teleconnections, at the different time and space scales, the climate dynamics of Venezuela and the region, and on the effectiveness of adaptation measures in general.

5 | Adaptation options

Reliable knowledge will be generated on three key aspects of the recent occurrence of extreme climate events capable of severely affecting the sustainability of human development and the preservation of the normal functioning of the main ecosystems present in the country and the region, namely:

  • Evolution and dynamics,
  • Origin and determinants, and
  • Forecast based on identified determinants and current trends.

6 | Key activities

  • Coordination between institutions.
  • Meetings between experts from different disciplines.
  • Generation of periodic climate bulletins.
  • Generation of climate services.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The prediction of emerging adverse scenarios is considered both a social option and an enabling measure aimed at fostering awareness of climate risks and vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

The achievement, at the national and regional levels, of food security, health security, environmental security and/or energy security, based on the timely and accurate identification of adaptation measures that help cope with the potential impacts generated by actual climate changes.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Rainfall anomaly indices (monthly basis, 1991-2020 climatology).
  • Sea surface temperature anomalies.
  • Monthly lagged cross-correlations.
  • Seasonal and annual trends.
  • Number of sectors that are users of climate information.
  • Number of sectors participating in the design and evaluation of climate services.
  • Number of climate bulletins generated.
  • Effectiveness of climate services.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • 1 document with the records of the strategies for coordination between institutions and meetings of experts from different disciplines.
  • 1 climate bulletin per year.
  • 3 sectors make use of climate services.

10 | Key actors

IVIC, MINEC, INAMEH, Universities and Research Centres.

A9. ESTABLISHMENT OF A COMMUNAL NETWORK FOR THE GENERATION OF TIMELY AND RELIABLE CLIMATOLOGICAL INFORMATION

Sector: Science and Technology

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The effectiveness and efficiency of an adaptation strategy depends directly on the quality of the available vulnerability information used in its design, implementation and monitoring. The quality of the information is determined by its reliability and level of detail (scale). Accordingly, there is a need for an efficient network for collecting climatological data throughout the national territory, from the country's 5336 communes.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

The general population, especially the inhabitants of the country's communes and communal circuits.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Generate timely information on vulnerability to extreme rainfall that makes it possible to design, implement and monitor efficient and effective adaptation strategies for human activities.

4 | Value proposition

Globally, the negative effects of climate change will intensify in the coming years. Reducing vulnerability and addressing loss and damage depend on mastery of climate information, its analysis and dissemination, in order to achieve an effective early warning system.

5 | Adaptation options

Generate reliable information in a transparent and dynamic manner at the level of hydrographic units that can be reviewed and updated regularly so as to allow the review and updating of the country's adaptation strategies.

6 | Key activities

  • Design and selection of communal weather stations to be installed.
  • Manufacture or acquisition of 5.336 meteorological measurement devices.
  • Training of specialized personnel to operate the weather stations in each commune.
  • Launch of the national communal system for meteorological data collection..

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The generation of timely and reliable information on vulnerability is considered both a social option and an enabling measure aimed at fostering awareness of climate risks and vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

Reliable and timely information will make it possible to avoid and/or address the most significant impacts of Climate Change.

At the same time, the implementation of adaptation strategies will generate jobs and reduce the inequities that the impacts of Climate Change inevitably generate.

9 | Key metrics

  • Vulnerability indicators according to the conceptual framework used by the IPCC, with geographical expression at the level of river basins.

10 | Key actors

Ministry of People's Power for Ecosocialism, Ministry of People's Power for Science and Technology.

A10. INCREASING THE RESILIENCE OF ECOSYSTEMS AND AGRO-PRODUCTIVE LIVELIHOODS OF THE COMMUNITIES OF THE PROTECTED ZONE OF THE TURIMIQUIRE MOUNTAIN MASSIF

Sector: Communes

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The Protected Zone of the Turimiquire Mountain Massif (ZPMMT) shows varying degrees of impact across its 540.000 hectares. This situation affects water resources, compromising the water and food security of the population of the states of Sucre, Anzoátegui, Monagas and Nueva Esparta. Torrential rains affecting the population have already occurred (the Cumanacoa case). Deforestation in the headwaters and slopes of the Manzanares and Neverí rivers, and others that feed the Los Clavellinos reservoir, which supplies water to this entire region.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: Population of the states of Sucre, Monagas, Anzoátegui and Nueva Esparta that benefits from the consumption of water from the reservoirs in the Turimiquire ZPMM. Rural communities engaged in subsistence agriculture. Small-scale producers (men and women). Communities of the middle and lower basins.

Users: Agricultural producers and communities located in the middle and lower basins, and the eastern population benefiting from the consumption of water from the reservoirs in the Turimiquire ZPMM.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Increase the resilience of ecosystems and agro-productive livelihoods of the communities of the protected zone of the Turimiquire mountain massif, as a programme with climate change adaptation strategies and actions.

4 | Value proposition

  • Increase the knowledge generated and disseminated on climate risk and adaptation actions.
  • Carry out strengthened knowledge management.
  • Develop a system for recording and monitoring damage from climate impacts.
  • Gather timely and usable climate information at the local level.
  • Design installed community early warning systems for floods and landslides.
  • Select key ecosystem areas for integrated water management
  • Prepare nurseries to produce 65 million plants in 5 years to reforest and rehabilitate at least 100 thousand hectares.
  • Promote resilient agro-productive practices and alternative livelihoods.

5 | Adaptation options

  • Capacity strengthening in vulnerable communities and institutional actors of the ZPMMT so that they know their climate risks and plan appropriate measures to manage and reduce them.
  • Implementation of community alert systems for preparedness and rapid response to disasters arising from flood and landslide impacts in the ZPMMT.
  • Restoration and conservation of degraded basins to develop greater moisture retention and forest cover, withstand the impacts of extreme events and variability, and support local livelihoods.
  • Strengthening of agro-productive livelihoods and diversification of the local economy.

6 | Key activities

  • Development of analyses and studies of climate risks in the ZPMMT and the vulnerability of ecosystems, communities and water resources to inform land-use planning and management plans with consideration of future scenarios.
  • Awareness-raising and training aimed at communities and national and local government technicians on climate change adaptation measures for the ZPMMT.
  • Support for the development of a system for recording and monitoring the impact on ecosystems, infrastructure and the livelihoods of the population from floods, landslides, fires and droughts.
  • Acquisition and installation of standardized hydrometeorological stations in Monagas, Anzoátegui and Sucre.
  • Training of technicians, institutional actors and local communities for the recording, use, interpretation and application of climate information and its dissemination in appropriate formats.
  • Install community early warning systems for floods and landslides.
  • Restoration, conservation and reforestation of degraded areas and community monitoring
  • Support for the development of community nurseries and a community network for the recovery of native seeds
  • Support for vulnerable farming communities in adopting resilient agro-productive practices.
  • Support for the transition to activities that make it possible to diversify livelihoods and markets to increase resilience.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

Increasing the Resilience of Ecosystems and Agro-Productive Livelihoods of the Communities of the Protected Zone of the Turimiquire Mountain Massif is considered both a physical and a social option that promotes community-based adaptation to increase resilience to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

Benefits:

  • Vulnerable communities and institutional actors of the ZPMMT know their climate risks and plan appropriate measures to manage and reduce them.
  • Improved preparedness and rapid response capacity for disasters arising from flood and landslide impacts in vulnerable communities of the ZPMMT.
  • Degraded basins with greater moisture retention and forest cover to withstand the impacts of extreme events and variability and support local livelihoods.
  • Livelihoods of vulnerable communities in the ZPMMT diversified to withstand the impacts of extreme events and climate variability. Co-benefits:
  • Economic: Reduction of the economic costs to the public and private sectors associated with climate impacts and improvement of tourism ecosystems.
  • Social: Social, environmental and gender safeguards and inclusive participation of vulnerable human groups.
  • Environmental: Improvement of air and soil quality, protection of biodiversity, carbon capture, improvement of ecosystem services, strengthening of food security and GHG mitigation.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Number of beneficiaries
  • % participation of rural women
  • Number of early warning systems designed.
  • Number of hydrometeorological stations installed.
  • Number of hydrometers installed.
  • Area of natural assets protected or rehabilitated.
  • Number of assets produced, developed, improved or strengthened
  • Number of beneficiaries (Direct and indirect

Targets (2025-2030):

  • Produce 65 million plants in nurseries in the 4 states considered
  • Intervene in 100.000 hectares with reforestation actions.
  • 6620 people benefiting from capacity strengthening.
  • Increase the participation of rural women in the fight against climate change to 50 %.

A11. FORMATION OF ECOSOCIALISM COUNCILS IN THE COMMUNES FOR THE FIGHT AGAINST CLIMATE CHANGE

Sector: Communes

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The exercise of environmental authority in the territory is limited by the reduced territorial impact of Government institutions. Therefore, popular organization in the country's communities needs to strengthen capacities to address the impacts of climate change from the Communes and Communal Councils, an ideal space for this, since they are the forms of social organization, so that they generate vulnerability reduction actions through the exercise of environmental authority within their territorial sphere.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: People's Power (social organizations, communal councils or communes) in areas vulnerable to climate change.

Users: People's Power (social organizations, communal councils or communes) in areas vulnerable to climate change, MINEC, MPPCMS.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Incorporate People's Power, through the ecosocialist committees of the communal councils and the Ecosocialism Councils in the Communes, into strategic decision-making that guarantees the continued drive toward socioeconomic development and the empowerment of communities in actions to fight climate change, within the framework of the public policies implemented in the national territory, on the path toward building a communal, popular and ecosocialist State.

4 | Value proposition

  • Take actions to strengthen the participation of People's Power in actions linked to the fight against climate change.
  • Increase the number of actors taking part in actions to address the climate crisis and environmental degradation.

5 | Adaptation options

The strengthening of People's Power in the country as an important factor in reducing vulnerability to Climate Change.

6 | Key activities

  • Development of Indicators to guide the assessment of the effects of Climate Change in the Communes and the actions undertaken by the Communal Councils, Social Battle Rooms and Social Movements.
  • In each Commune, Communal Council, Social Battle Room and Social Movement, an Ecosocialist Committee must be formed, made up of spokespersons (men and women) who permanently monitor the adverse effects of climate change and build the action proposal to address the fight against climate change.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures The implementation of climate empowerment action programmes for People's Power constitutes a social option and an enabling measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8| Benefits and co-benefits

  • Protection of the general population against floods or droughts.
  • Provide People's Power with tools that can contribute to the fight against climate change through concrete actions.

  • Number of communal [councils] registered with an ecosocialist committee formed.

Biological Diversity Sector

A12. STRENGTHENING OF CAPACITIES FOR BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY MANAGEMENT

Sector: Biological Diversity

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The main causes of biological diversity loss are deforestation, destruction and fragmentation of ecosystems, unsustainable use of wild flora and fauna, introduction and establishment of invasive species, land-use changes, pollution and climate change (ENCDB 2010- 2020). On average, around 25 % of species in assessed animal and plant groups are threatened, which suggests that around one million species are already threatened with extinction, many within just decades (Kuming - Montreal, 2022). Climate change has a significant impact on biological diversity. It constitutes a threat to ecosystems, species and genetic resources; moreover, impacts on biodiversity can alter the structure and functioning of ecosystems and their interactions with biological, geochemical and hydrological cycles (IPCC, 2007).

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: The population living in the different bioregions of the national territory, made up of local communities and Indigenous peoples. Users: Government Bodies and Institutions, Academia, Research Centres, Foundations and Non-governmental Organizations.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

The Ministry of People's Power for Ecosocialism (MINEC) has the mission of protecting, conserving and restoring the environment to guarantee the sustainable use and exploitation of natural resources, respecting the processes and cycles of nature; it therefore carries out actions for the conservation of biological diversity through the development and implementation of management plans, programmes and projects, protocols and actions for ecosystem restoration and the conservation of wild fauna and flora, both in situ and ex situ, with the active participation of governmental and non-governmental bodies and institutions, the private sector, local communities and Indigenous peoples, including women, girls and young people, within the framework of the National Strategy for the Conservation of Biological Diversity 2024-2030 and its Action Plan.

4 | Value proposition

  • Development and implementation of education and training programmes on the conservation of biological diversity and natural protected areas.
  • Development of conservation programmes and projects for wild fauna and flora species.
  • Preparation and updating of the land-use plans and use regulations of natural protected areas for the conservation of biological diversity (wildlife refuges, reserves and sanctuaries; biosphere reserves).

5 | Adaptation options - Education and training on the importance of biological diversity conservation. - Determine the degree of threat to species and ecosystems. - Restoration of degraded habitats and recovery of populations of wild flora and fauna species.

6 | Key activities

  • Hold outreach workshops for the implementation of the National Strategy for the Conservation of Biological Diversity 2024- 2030 and its Action Plan.
  • Development and implementation of conservation programmes for wild flora and fauna species, with an emphasis on threatened or endangered species, carried out under the direct or indirect supervision of MINEC through the General Directorate of Biological Diversity, aimed at protecting, conserving and reinforcing populations of wild fauna and flora species, for which in situ and ex situ conservation actions are carried out.

The National Programme for the Conservation of Threatened Species includes the following projects: Fauna

  • Conservation of sea turtles (Dermochelys coriácea, Chelonia mydas, Eretmochelys imbricata, Caretta caretta and Lepidochelys olivácea).
  • Conservation of the arrau turtle (Podocnemis expansa) and other continental chelonians.
  • Conservation of the Orinoco crocodile (Crocodylus intermedias).
  • Conservation of the American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus).
  • Conservation of the spectacled bear (Tremarctus ornatos).
  • Conservation of the jaguar (Panthera onca).
  • Conservation of the tapir(7ap/rus terrestris). Flora
  • Conservation of the Caracas walnut (Juglans venezuelensis).
  • Conservation of moriche palm swamps (Mauritia flexuosa).
  • Conservation of mangroves (Rhizophora mangle).
  • Conservation of non-timber flora species (mosses, tree ferns, frailejón, orchids, bromeliads).

These projects include the following actions: habitat protection, safeguarding of nests, transplanting of nests at risk of flooding or predation, breeding and cultivation of specimens in ex situ conservation centres, reintroduction of specimens into the wild through the release or planting of specimens in their natural distribution areas; this in order to restore the populations of threatened species.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The strengthening of capacities for biological diversity management is considered both a physical and a social option for adaptation to climate change, since it includes both ecosystem-based adaptation criteria and social instruments for raising awareness among communities and society in general. This strengthening is considered a direct measure to reduce the vulnerability and increase the resilience of ecosystems and their biological diversity to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8| Benefits and co-benefits

Biological diversity, in its three components, ecosystems, species and genetic resources, provides a great number of benefits to human communities, including climate regulation, water resources, carbon capture, air and water purification, flood prevention, access to food and other essential resources, such as the active ingredients found in plants for medicines, and recreation sites.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • No. of training activities carried out.
  • No. of outreach activities carried out.
  • No. of people educated and trained
  • No. of seeds collected per species.
  • No. of specimens per species grown in nurseries.
  • No. of specimens per species planted (threatened and endangered species).
  • No. of specimens per species bred.
  • No. of specimens per species released.
  • No. of land-use plans and use regulations prepared.
  • No. of land-use plans and use regulations updated.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • 500 outreach activities carried out.
  • 20 training activities carried out.
  • 10.000 people educated and trained.
  • 24.500 seeds collected per species.
  • 2.800 specimens per species grown in nurseries.
  • 700 specimens per species planted.
  • 140.000 specimens per species bred.
  • 140.000 specimens per species released.
  • 4 Land-Use Plans and Use Regulations prepared.
  • 1 Land-Use Plan and Use Regulations updated.

Ecosystems Sector

A13. STRENGTHENING OF THE INTEGRATED MANAGEMENT OF THE PUBLIC DOMAIN OF VENEZUELA'S COASTAL ZONES

Sector: Ecosystems

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

Coastal zones constitute a unique space of great natural interest for the development of various uses. This strip constitutes a specific area of special sensitivity within the coastal zone that is subject to the impacts of climate change due to sea level rise (SLR). Flood-prone areas in Venezuelan coastal zones include spaces declared as Areas Under Special Administration Regime (ABRAE). In parallel, the impact values of the five Venezuelan wetlands declared as Ramsar sites. Increased variability of mean sea level is considered a socio-natural hazard, especially with its potential impacts on population centres such as Maracaibo, Lagunillas - Bachaqueros, San Juan de Los Cayos, Chichiriviche, Tucacas, Puerto Cabello, Higuerote, San José de Rio Chico, Boca de Uchire - Puerto Píritu, Puerto La Cruz, Lecherías, Cumaná, Morro de Puerto Santo, Tucupita Las Piedras, Guamache, San Pedro de Coche, among others. In this context, the management of blue ecosystems (mangroves, seagrasses) and sandy beaches are considered fundamental strategies for adaptation to climate change.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: Directly, 18% (6.136.317 inhabitants) of the Venezuelan population living within the limits of Venezuela's coastal zones.

Users: Coastal Communal Councils, Tourism and Recreational Service Providers, Fishers, Aquaculture Producers, Coastal Mayors' Offices and State Governments, Central and State Working Committees for Coastal Zones, Civil Protection, Fire Departments, MINEC, INPARQUES, INSOPESCA, MPPT-INEA, MINTUR, MPPRIJP, TIFM, MPPD, IPC, FUNVISIS, MPPRE.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

The Strengthening of the Integrated Management of the Public Domain of Venezuela's Coastal Zones represents one of the principles contained in the Draft Territorial Planning and Integrated Management of the Coastal Zones of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela ( 2014) and has its guidelines through the public domain spaces programme, which includes two subprogrammes (delimitation and demarcation of public domain areas and sustainable management of sandy beaches), and likewise in the vulnerable zones programme, which is also made up of two subprogrammes (areas vulnerable to socio-natural and technological hazards, and adaptation to climate change). The importance of the public domain of Venezuela's coastal zones lies in the capacity of this space to buffer the effects of natural processes from land to sea and from sea to land, especially the effects resulting from climate change such as sea level rise and the increased frequency and intensity of meteorological phenomena such as hurricanes and storms.

4 | Value proposition

  • Recognition of key spaces linked to the public domain, such as: coastal lagoons, mangroves, other wetlands, sandy beaches, among others.
  • Identification of the occupation processes of the public domain areas of Venezuela's coastal zones.
  • Technical, administrative and legal definition of the public domain strip of the Venezuelan coastal zone.
  • Zoning of the public domain strip of the Venezuelan coastal zones.
  • Establishment of directives and guidelines for the management of the public domain strip of the Venezuelan coastal zones.
  • Raise awareness of the importance of Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) and the technical capacities for its implementation, through the implementation of the Marine Spatial Plan.
  • Incorporate climate change into any planning and land-use study as a key element within the integrated coastal zone management process.

5 | Adaptation options

The Ministry of People's Power for Ecosocialism (MINEC), as National Environmental Authority and Coordinator of the land-use planning and integrated management processes for coastal zones, will manage, together with the Central and State Working Committees for Coastal Zones and with the participation of People's Power bodies, the planning-action mechanisms that drive strategies for the sustainable management and recovery of the public domain and sandy beaches, as well as Marine Spatial Planning (MSP), in order to address sea level rise processes as an effect of climate change and reduce socio-natural and socio-environmental risks in the Venezuelan coastal zones.

6 | Key activities

  • Updating of the methodology for the Physical-Natural Inventory and Characterization, diagnosis and mapping of the Sandy Beaches of Venezuela.
  • Identify the structures located within the spaces linked to the public domain and analyse the feasibility of relocation.
  • Delimitation of the land strip of the public domain space of Venezuela's 14 coastal states.
  • Identify and assess the areas to be remediated within the public domain in the coastal zones.
  • Assess potential actions to promote the stabilization of beaches and dunes, the construction of works to limit the transport capacity of incident waves, and artificial sediment nourishment.
  • Define and analyse the existing and plausible future conditions of the marine and coastal environment, and marine and coastal uses (opportunities and threats).
  • Map natural resources, socioeconomic activities and cultural values using Participatory GIS, including the potential impacts of climate change, at appropriate spatial scales; incorporate the results of previous coastal vulnerability assessments.
  • Build capacities and skill sets so that the relevant stakeholders participate in the planning process.
  • Develop, with a participatory approach, marine and coastal spatial plans that include scenarios for zoning areas for multiple use, limited use and no-fishing areas based on the results of stakeholder consultations and simulations of plausible future conditions (including climate change), paying close attention to the influences on the coastal and marine environment of processes associated with the land-water interface (source-sea).
  • Develop cultivation and planting programmes for red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle), black mangrove (Avicennia germinans) and white mangrove (Laguncularia racemosa), coconut palms (Cocos nucifera) and Batis Marítima.
  • Establish directives and guidelines oriented toward the sustainable use of this space in order to regulate activities in accordance with the legal framework in force and its environmental characteristics.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The Strengthening of the Integrated Management of the Public Domain of Venezuela's Coastal Zones is considered an institutional option and an enabling measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

The management of the public domain space of coastal zones constitutes a complex process that seeks to give continuity and specificity to the land-use planning and integrated management work promoted since 2004; it also involves various actors and interests, which base their actions on the legal foundations and planning instruments in force; likewise, it seeks to respond to the calls established through international agreements such as: CBD, Ramsar, Kunming-Montreal, the Ocean Decade, among others.

For the above reasons, it is necessary to achieve effective and efficient management of the public domain space and the seas, through the development of a methodology for the delimitation of these zones and the development of a series of guidelines that make it possible to reduce conflicts between public and private actors and to re-establish the public utility character of this space in accordance with the provisions of the Decree with Force of Law on Coastal Zones and the Draft Land-Use Planning and Management Plan for the Coastal Zones of Venezuela.

Likewise, the information generated from the characterization and inventory of Venezuela's sandy beaches will make it possible to formulate specific management tools for these spaces, with the intention of updating the methodology for their proper management in light of the challenges generated by the variability of mean sea level.

Within the framework of sustainable management of the Venezuelan coastal landscape, there is a heterogeneous mosaic of land-use and vegetation covers, with different degrees of intervention that may be of special importance for connectivity, to enhance the capacity of the territory and favour flows of species or groups of species through landscape diversity. To this end, it is necessary to enhance the conservation and sustainable use of the biodiversity of certain areas, not necessarily protected, that can act as ecological corridors, and nature-based solutions, in addition to enabling communication between spaces for the genetic exchange of flora and fauna, as well as the development of livelihoods of coastal communities.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Number of methodologies developed/proposed.
  • Delimited area of land public domain.
  • Number of instruments designed for the management and functionality of the public domain.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • Updating of the methodology for the Inventory and Characterization of the Sandy Beaches of Venezuela.
  • One (01) Methodological proposal aimed at the delimitation of the public domain areas of Venezuela's coastal zones.
  • Delimitation of the land public domain of Venezuela's 14 coastal states.
  • Fourteen (14) instruments for the management and functionality of the public domain as a defined space to buffer the effects of natural processes from land to sea and from sea to land.
  • One (01) Methodological proposals and the development of Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) for the Gulf of Paria and the Deltaic - Atlantic Region.

M14. STRENGTHENING OF MANAGEMENT TO COMBAT THE THREATS OF AQUATIC INVASIVE ALIEN SPECIES IN VENEZUELA

Sector: Ecosystems

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The introduction and spread of invasive alien species (IAS) in marine and coastal environments in Venezuela have caused negative impacts on biological diversity, marine-coastal ecosystems and ecosystem services, which are increased by limitations in institutional and community capacities to address this problem. Coastal zones are particularly affected by relative sea level rise, coastal erosion, rising sea temperatures and the increased frequency of hurricanes as consequences of climate change. This affects the spread and establishment of many alien species, increasing their invasion potential, reducing the resilience of habitats to biological invasions and intensifying their impacts on the environment.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Direct beneficiaries: Fishing communities, local and national authorities, government institutions, women's groups in productive activities, environmental NGOs, universities and research centres, Local population in vulnerable areas.

Indirect beneficiaries: Tourists and communities of neighbouring countries, by preventing the spread of IAS to other regions of the Caribbean.

Users: Local communities, Specialized technicians, Educational institutions, MINEC, INPARQUES, MINPESCA and key actors from the public and private sectors.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Reduce biodiversity loss and the impairment of marine-coastal ecosystem services in Venezuela, strengthening capacities for the management of aquatic IAS, with a gender approach, and promoting strategies

for ecosystem restoration and sustainable productive alternatives. By implementing the adaptation measures, it is expected to obtain ecosystems more resilient to climate change, greater participation of

communities, improved livelihoods of local communities, better environmental governance and long-term food security.

4 | Value proposition

  • It is a tangible solution to the degradation of the reef ecosystem and the decline of its fishery resources, through a management model that combines the traditional knowledge of fishers (men and women) with the best scientific practices.
  • It has a positive impact on food security through the conservation of biodiversity and the restoration of marine and coastal ecosystems. It enables the diversification and strengthening of livelihoods through the implementation of sustainable productive practices.
  • Improvement of environmental governance and technical capacities at the national and local levels, establishing a coordinated system for the management of aquatic IAS.
  • It recognizes and promotes the role of women as fundamental managers and guardians in the care of natural resources.

5 | Adaptation options

  • Improvement of ABRAE management in the 5 key MCPAs affected by aquatic IAS.
  • Economic valuation of the 5 key MCPAs for the impact of aquatic IAS on ecosystem services.
  • National System for the Monitoring and Control of Invasive Alien Species (SINCEEI) with community participation.
  • Restoration of areas affected by aquatic IAS in the 5 key MCPAs.
  • Implementation of socio-productive alternatives as livelihoods to mitigate or offset the impact of IAS on local communities.
  • Gender plan with the contribution of women to reducing biological diversity loss and adapting to climate change.

6 | Key activities

  • Proposal to update the PORU of five key MCPAs (Mochima NP, Henry Pittier NP, San Esteban NP, Morrocoy NP and Cuare WR) incorporating the management of aquatic IAS, the restoration of coral environments and the implementation of sustainable productive practices, as an adaptive response to climate change. The reactivation of tide gauge stations for monitoring marine climate parameters is envisaged.
  • Use of the modified Protocol of the Alternative Ecosystem Services Valuation Approach (AESVA), in order to assess the economic impact of the IAS Unomia stolonifera in the five key MCPAs. It is a proposal that merges different areas of knowledge, namely: environmental economics, marketing, climate change, and formulation and evaluation of economic projects.
  • Design of strategies to improve IAS management. Coordinate strategies with community participation (environmental brigades, which include activities linked to the prevention, early warning, control and eradication of IAS, as well as monitoring the effects of climate change on marine ecosystems, among other functions).
  • Removal of Unomia stolonifera over 500.000 m and ecological restoration of 100.000 m of area affected by this IAS.
  • The project will develop a pilot restoration programme with native coral species. Likewise, a programme will be implemented to improve local competencies on the restoration of coral reefs recovered from the U. stolonifera invasion, with the aim of bringing these environments to a condition as close as possible to the one they had before being affected. At least 15 courses on restoration are planned, and they will be placed in a virtual environment to guarantee their dissemination and the continuity of training.
  • Implementation of a community training programme on sustainable productive practices in aquaculture, agroecology, processing of fishery and agricultural products, ecotourism and business management. Likewise, courses on the interpretation of climate parameters and their influence on fishing patterns and safe navigation.
  • Women are encouraged to take part in forming the environmental brigades and in local community organizations, as fundamental managers and guardians in the care of natural resources.
  • Knowledge-sharing meetings will also be held in order to value their knowledge of local ecosystems and their needs, highlighting their contribution to fisheries management and strengthening their capacities for conservation, sustainable development and the management of aquatic invasive alien species. Likewise, enterprises in which women contribute to addressing environmental challenges and food production will be encouraged.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The strengthening of management to combat the threats of aquatic invasive alien species in Venezuela is considered a physical option and a direct (implementing) measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • Increased resilience of aquatic ecosystems, reduced coastal vulnerability, reduced biodiversity loss, increased carbon sequestration.
  • Improved livelihoods, empowerment of women in sustainable productive activities, strengthened adaptive capacity to climate change, improved food security and poverty reduction.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Number of updated PORU proposals.
  • Number of valuations.
  • Change in the economic value of the 5 key MCPAs due to the impact of IAS on ecosystem services.
  • Number of IAS management strategies developed or improved.
  • Number of environmental brigades created and linked to IAS management strategies.
  • Area undergoing restoration.
  • Number of communities involved in restoration activities.
  • Number of pilot sustainable productive practices implemented.
  • Number of courses delivered.
  • Number of people trained.
  • Number of women involved in IAS management.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • Preparation of five PORU update proposals.
  • Economic valuations of five MCPAs.
  • Development or improvement of four IAS management strategies.
  • Creation and coordination of 10 environmental brigades, with participation of 40 % of the population being women and five of young people and children.
  • Five hectares of marine-coastal ecosystem undergoing restoration.
  • 100 inhabitants involved in restoration activities.
  • Implementation of 15 pilot sustainable productive practices.
  • 60 training courses delivered.
  • 300 people trained.
  • 120 women involved in IAS management.

101 Key actors

MINEC, MINPESCA, MINTUR, INPARQUES; MINCYT, INEA, MINMU3ER, local authorities, local communities, fishers, NGOs, universities, tourists, international organizations.

Coordination Mechanisms: Formation of an inter-institutional working group for the management of aquatic IAS, with a gender approach.

Policies and Regulatory Framework: Updating of regulations on aquatic IAS and strengthening of legislation on marine-coastal protected areas.

A15. INTEGRATED MANAGEMENT OF SUSTAINABLE LANDSCAPES FOR THE CONSERVATION OF THE AMAZON FOREST BIOME

Sector: Ecosystems

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

In the Amazon forest biome, neither the biological diversity nor the food and productive potential of Amazonian palms and trees is utilized. Likewise, conuco agriculture is of low profitability, and there is weak knowledge and appreciation of biological diversity, together with a lack of integration of scientific, traditional, local and ancestral knowledge, including in decision-making.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: Five Indigenous communities of the Protected Zone of the Cataniapo River basin, distributed along four [in the] Orinoco-Cuao-Sipapo-Autana axis and one in San Carlos de Río Negro, and biological diversity.

Users: Communities, MINEC, INPARQUES, MPPPI and key actors from the public and private sectors.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Design and implement community action plans for co-management in ABRAE, including ecosystem-based adaptation solutions.

4 | Value proposition

  • Strengthen land-use management with an ecological approach for the conservation of ecosystems and biological diversity, and the implementation of sustainable, inclusive and resilient agri-food systems adapted to climate change, which is designed to support the implementation of an ambitious climate change strategy between 2022- 2031.
  • Increase the visibility of and investment in these solutions, contributing to low-carbon economies while guaranteeing sufficient, safe and nutritious food for healthy diets, as well as other agricultural products and services, for present and future generations.

5 | Adaptation options

  • Agroforestry systems.
  • Traditional Indigenous crops.
  • Water storage.
  • Inclusion of aquaculture production systems.
  • Native seed bank.
  • Management of melipona bees.

6 | Key activities

  • Design and implement community action plans for the prioritized Indigenous communities.
  • Design and implementation of community extension programmes.
  • Monitoring and evaluation.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The integrated management of sustainable landscapes for the conservation of the Amazon forest biome is considered a physical option and a direct (implementing) measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

Direct benefits:

  • Improvement and diversification of the livelihoods of the prioritized Indigenous communities.

Additional benefits:

  • Economic (Indigenous communities).
  • Sociocultural (gender and intercultural approach).
  • Environmental (conservation of biological diversity and its ecosystem services).

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Community action plans for restoration and co-management in ABRAE designed and implemented.
  • Multiple-use forest or fruit plantations for conservation in ABRAE.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • 11 participatory community action plans for restoration and co-management in ABRAE.
  • 700 ha actively restored by the communities through multiple-use forest or fruit plantations for conservation in ABRAE.
  • 500 ha restored through agroforestry systems in ABRAE.
  • 50 ha of landscapes under improved practices with communities in areas outside ABRAE.

A16. CREATION OF SCHOOL TRAINING PROGRAMMES ON THE MANAGEMENT AND PRACTICAL ACTION OF ECOSOCIALISM

Sector: Basic Education

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

In the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, education is recognized as an essential human right and a key pillar for the social and economic development of the nation. The country's education system strives to form critical, ethical and participatory citizens who are able to contribute significantly to the progress and well-being of society. One of the greatest current challenges is climate change; for education it implies a challenge in which values must be redefined, the development of environmental awareness consolidated, and modes of action, habits and social skills changed, so that they express environmentally friendly behaviours. In this regard, and in compliance with the provisions of the Constitution of the Republic (article 107) and the Organic Law on the Environment (article 34), the strengthening of national experiences in the management and practical construction of ecosocialism should be considered.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: Students and Teachers, General Population. Users: Students and Teachers, General Population, MPPE, MINEC, Mayors' Offices, State Governments.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Incorporate pedagogical strategies as an element of management and construction in the practice of ecosocialism, for the strengthening of the guiding principles and values for decision-making and actions that contribute to the fight against the climate crisis.

4 | Value proposition

  • Establish education-extension programmes for the fight against climate change, aimed at girls, boys, adolescents and young people so that they commit to climate action in their communities and participate in climate policy processes at the regional, national and international levels. This includes, among other priorities, recognition of the importance of developing green skills that help them prepare for a sustainable future and a just transition toward a future of a changing climate.
  • Recognize the actions and research of educational institutions that promote, help understand and improve possible solutions that counteract the effects of climate change.

5 | Adaptation options

Didactic and practical strategies that make it possible to strengthen the guiding principles and values for decision-making and actions that contribute to the fight against the climate crisis.

6 | Key activities

  • Preparation of booklets, pedagogical magazines and videos on climate change.
  • Education and training of school environmental brigades.
  • Management of learning communities.
  • Field activities and guided pedagogical expeditions for students on the effects caused by climate change.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The management and practical construction of ecosocialism constitutes a social option and an enabling measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • Raise students' awareness of the importance of the principles of co-responsibility and citizen participation in environmental conservation and the management of the climate crisis.
  • Changes in behaviours, attitudes and culture regarding the conservation of natural resources and the climate crisis.
  • Applicability of environmental education and education for sustainable development in professional performance and the transmission of environmental awareness to new generations.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Number of students educated and trained.
  • Number of people involved in the fight against the climate crisis.
  • Number of educational communities involved.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • Students educated and trained: 750.000.
  • Teachers involved: 375.000
  • Educational Communities involved: 250.000

MPPE, MINEC, Educational Institutions and Communities.

A17. MAINSTREAMING ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION AND CLIMATE CRISIS MANAGEMENT INTO UNIVERSITY EDUCATION CURRICULA

Sector: Higher Education

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

In the country's public universities, 125 degree-granting programs are offered that are linked to building capacities to combat climate change; these include Agroecology, Environmental Management, Environmental Sciences, Environmental Engineering, among others. Meanwhile, in the private sphere, this academic offering comprises 41 programs, linked to Environmental and Natural Resources Engineering, Environmental Engineering, Environmental Technology, Renewable Natural Resources Conservation Technology, Environmental Studies, among others. Accordingly, university education constitutes a strategic pillar for adaptation to climate change and the mitigation of its effects in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. Through academic training, applied research and the promotion of environmental awareness, the sector seeks to integrate climate knowledge into higher education in order to create sustainable solutions that respond to national needs.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: University students and professors, the general population. Users: University Students and Professors, the General Population, MPPEU, MINEC, Mayors' Offices, Governorates.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Formulation of strategies that promote coordinated work between the Venezuelan State and communities. This initiative will make it possible to create networks among the actors involved so that they carry out actions that increase adaptive capacity and resilience to climate change.

4 | Value proposition

  • Creation of working groups, composed of officials from this Ministerial Body and from university education institutions, in order to contribute actively to the process of adaptation to climate change.
  • Consider strengthening networks of university education institutions in order to contribute actively to the process of adaptation to climate change.
  • Evaluate university regulations in order to integrate environmental training into the requirements for promotion in rank.
  • Strengthen national environmental training chairs, and gradually build a more aware culture around the subject.
  • Improve student access to degree programs with an environmental protection vision, in all states of the country.

5 | Adaptation options

Mainstreaming environmental education and climate crisis management into higher education curricula.

6 | Key activities

  • Request from the corresponding working groups quarterly reports containing information on the actions taken to increase the resilience and capacity of the population to adapt to climate change, emphasizing the need to build strategies that lead to a constant exchange of information between the Universities, the Ministry and the communities.
  • Propose schedules of possible dynamic meetings between University Education institutions and community leaders focused on environmental issues.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

Mainstreaming environmental education and climate crisis management into higher education curricula constitutes a social option and an enabling measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • Raise students' awareness of the importance of the principles of co-responsibility and citizen participation in environmental conservation and the management of the climate crisis.
  • Changes in behaviours, attitudes and culture regarding the conservation of natural resources and the climate crisis.
  • Applicability of environmental education and education for sustainable development in professional performance and the transmission of environmental awareness to new generations.

  • Number of students in the area of environmental management and climate change.
  • Number of university networks formed in the field of environmental management and climate change.
  • Number of university regulations incorporating competencies in the field of environmental management and climate change as a promotion requirement.

Electric Power Sector

A18. NATIONAL PLAN FOR ADAPTATION TO CLIMATE CHANGE IN THE ELECTRICITY SECTOR

Sector: Electric Power

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The national electricity generation matrix is mainly hydroelectric and, to a lesser extent, thermoelectric (gas), so it is directly exposed to variations in precipitation rates and temperature increases, which makes it highly vulnerable to extreme weather events such as heavy rainfall and prolonged droughts that directly affect energy generation capacity. An example of this is the decline in reservoir levels, a direct consequence of prolonged drought periods, which compromises and endangers the stability of the electricity supply. Even though the State has invested in the recovery, maintenance and upgrading of its infrastructure, as well as in the implementation of new, more environmentally friendly energy sources for electricity generation, its capacity to adapt continues to be limited largely by the sanctions and unilateral coercive measures on the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, which have prevented it from overcoming existing technological obsolescence, as well as the upgrading and implementation of new infrastructure adapted to the current and future climate scenario, endangering energy security and consequently the most vulnerable populations of the country.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: The electricity sector, the Public and Private Sector, the entire general population.

Users: Isolated, indigenous and border communities, Children and adolescents, Older adults, the Electricity Sector, the Public and Private Sector, the Entire general population.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

The strategy proposes developing a National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change in the Electricity Sector, including medium- and long-term measures to strengthen the sector in order to increase its resilience to extreme weather events and anthropogenic disturbances. The objective is to improve prevention, response and recovery capacity, guaranteeing the continuity and sustainability of the electricity service.

4 | Value proposition

The value proposition addresses the design, development and implementation of the Adaptation Plan, which will allow the Electricity Sector to increase its adaptive capacity and resilience, in order to avoid or reduce present and future damage arising from both the climate crisis and anthropogenic events. It also aims to achieve long-term sustainability, guaranteeing the security and continuity of the electricity supply and safeguarding the country's economic and social development.

5 | Adaptation options

In order to increase adaptive capacity in the sector, enabling (soft) measures will be established relating to the development of a governance framework for climate change adaptation in the electricity sector and the strengthening of human capacities to face the adverse effects of the climate crisis, such as: research and development, training and awareness-raising, cooperation and financing, among other actions.

6 | Key activities

The design and development of the National Adaptation Plan, which includes: Establishment of the governance framework and strengthening of institutional capacities in: research into new, less polluting sources of electricity generation, training (reservoir management under extreme climate conditions, strengthening of the preventive trimming and pruning plan for cases of fires or interruption of power lines, among others), awareness-raising and dissemination on Eco-energy management, Comprehensive assessment of the vulnerability and risk of the electricity system to extreme events (floods, droughts, storms, forest fires, landslides, among others), Analysis of future climate scenarios, Identification of loss and damage from extreme weather and anthropogenic events, Identification and planning of medium- and long-term adaptation measures, Implementation and monitoring of the Plan.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change in the Electricity Sector is considered an institutional option and an enabling measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

Direct benefits: Increased adaptive capacity of the electricity sector to extreme weather events, Improved management of electrical infrastructure (generation, transmission and distribution) in the event of extreme weather events, Minimization of interruptions in the electricity supply, Improved energy efficiency in the core processes of the National Electric System (SEN).

Additional benefits: Greater energy security, Strengthening of the health, education, agri-food and tourism sectors, among others. Improvements in livelihoods associated with the electricity service.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators: Number of institutional arrangements for climate governance in the electric power sector, Number of climate change vulnerability analyses carried out, Number of watersheds prioritized for the proposal of climate change adaptation measures, Number of climate change adaptation measures proposed.

Targets (2025-2030): 01 document of institutional arrangements arrangements for climate governance in the electric power sector, 04 climate change vulnerability analyses carried out, 02 watersheds prioritized for the proposal of climate change adaptation measures.

101 Key actors

Ministries of People's Power for Ecosocialism (MINEC), Electric Power (MPPEE), Water Affairs (MINAGUAS), Communes, Planning, Foreign Affairs, Foreign Trade, and Economy and Finance.

1.000.000 US$.

A19. EDUCATION AND ENERGY EFFICIENCY PLAN

Sector: Electric Power

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The national electricity generation matrix is mainly hydroelectric and, to a lesser extent, thermoelectric (gas), so it is directly exposed to variations in precipitation rates and temperature increases, which makes it highly vulnerable to extreme weather events such as heavy rainfall and prolonged droughts that directly affect energy generation capacity. An example of this is the decline in reservoir levels, a direct consequence of prolonged drought periods, which compromises and endangers the stability of the electricity supply. Even though the State has invested in the recovery, maintenance and upgrading of its infrastructure, as well as in the implementation of new, more environmentally friendly energy sources for electricity generation, its capacity to adapt continues to be limited largely by the sanctions and unilateral coercive measures on the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, which have prevented it from overcoming existing technological obsolescence, as well as the upgrading and implementation of new infrastructure adapted to the current and future climate scenario, endangering energy security and consequently the most vulnerable populations of the country. In this regard, the participation of all the country's communities in the rational and efficient use of energy in their homes and workplaces is necessary, in order to achieve energy savings that contribute to reducing the consequences of climate impacts.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: The electricity sector, the Public and Private Sector, the entire general population.

Users: Isolated, indigenous and border communities, Children and adolescents, Older adults, the Electricity Sector, the Public and Private Sector, the Entire general population.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Foster a culture of sustainability through transformative education that empowers all citizens to make informed decisions and take concrete actions in favor of energy and environmental efficiency, together with solid inter-institutional collaboration and a comprehensive curriculum (Diploma courses, Instructional guides, Conferences, Workshops), in order to achieve a society that is more aware and resilient to the challenges of climate change, contributing to reduced electricity consumption.

4 | Value proposition

The value proposition addresses the design, development and implementation of the Energy Efficiency Plan from a climate change adaptation perspective, integrating the concepts of energy efficiency and reduced consumption into the nation's educational processes, as a means to achieve long-term sustainability, guaranteeing the security and continuity of the electricity supply and safeguarding the country's economic and social development.

5 | Adaptation options

In order to increase adaptive capacity in the sector, enabling (soft) measures will be established relating to the strengthening of human capacities to face the adverse effects of the climate crisis, such as: research and development, training and awareness-raising, cooperation and financing, among other actions.

6 | Key activities

  • Online Seminars: Develop online platforms with open and free educational resources.
  • Citizen participation: Involve local communities in the design and evaluation of educational programs, ensuring that they respond to the needs and priorities of each region.
  • Strengthening research: Focused on technology for energy saving and optimization of energy use.
  • Development of outreach campaigns: On the rational and efficient use of energy and the development of a culture.
  • Implementation and monitoring of the Plan.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change in the Electricity Sector is considered an institutional option and an enabling measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

Direct benefits:

  • Increased adaptive capacity of the electricity sector to extreme weather events.
  • Improved management of electrical infrastructure (generation, transmission and distribution) in the event of extreme weather events.
  • Minimization of interruptions in the electricity supply.
  • Improved energy efficiency in the core processes of the National Electric System (SEN).

Additional benefits:

  • Greater energy security.
  • Strengthening of sectors such as: health, education, agri-food, tourism, among others.
  • Improvements in livelihoods associated with the electricity service.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Number of awareness-raising activities.
  • Number of attendees at awareness-raising activities.
  • Number of research studies carried out.
  • Number of outreach campaigns.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • 01 document of institutional arrangements for climate governance in the electric power sector.
  • 04 climate change vulnerability analyses carried out.
  • 02 watersheds prioritized for the proposal of climate change adaptation measures.

101 Key actors

Ministries of People's Power for Ecosocialism, Electric Power, Communes, Education, University Education, Communication and Information, Foreign Affairs, Foreign Trade, Economy and Finance, Habitat and Housing, Science and Technology, Industry and National Production.

A20. PROMOTION OF ENVIRONMENTAL CULTURE TO ADDRESS THE CLIMATE CRISIS

Sector: Ecosocialist Training

Context analysis

1 Problem definition

In recent decades, environmental problems arising from anthropogenic activities have intensified the global triple planetary crisis, which includes the climate crisis. In response, Venezuela promotes environmental education activities, enshrined in the Constitution of the Republic (article 107) and in the Organic Law on the Environment (article 34), which state that environmental education is mandatory in the education system and in non-formal citizen education. Accordingly, it is necessary to strengthen strategies that promote environmental awareness and culture among the People's Power.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: People's Power, children and adolescents in their communities, the public and private sector.

Users: The Venezuelan population in general, MINEC, Mayors' Offices, Governorates.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Promote environmental culture, through environmental education campaigns, enabling the fostering of values for environmental management and conservation as well as the exchange of knowledge and the collective construction of actions

to address the climate crisis.

4 | Value proposition

  • Engage children, young people and adults with pedagogical strategies relating to climate change adaptation and the related thematic areas.
  • Develop awareness-raising spaces for the People's Power, through specialized training sessions on the 3 thematic areas (environmental management, integrated waste management, and preservation of life and biological diversity).
  • Develop an awareness-raising campaign aimed at the public and private sector.

5 | Adaptation options

Formulation and implementation of an Environmental Education Campaign to address the Climate Crisis.

6 | Key activities

  • Development of the structure, content and methodology of the campaign.
  • Incorporation of the campaign into digital and traditional media.
  • Promotion of the campaign through in situ outreach aimed at beneficiaries and users.
  • Capacity building for the promoting team of the awareness-raising program against the climate crisis.
  • Follow-up of the Environmental Education Campaign.
  • Create a knowledge network on environmental education. • Evaluation of the impact generated by the Environmental Education Campaign.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The Environmental Education Campaign to address the Climate Crisis constitutes a social option and an enabling measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

  • Raise awareness among actors regarding production and consumption patterns.
  • Strengthening of public management.
  • Reduction of environmental pollution.

  • Number of annual training activities.
  • Number of environmental education activities per year.
  • Number of people sensitized per year.

  • 48 annual training activities in the territory to promote the awareness-raising program against the climate crisis.

  • 51.840 people sensitized annually (60 people on average per activity).

A21. NATIONAL AWARENESS-RAISING PLAN AGAINST THE CLIMATE CRISIS

Sector: Ecosocialist Training

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The National Awareness-Raising Plan against the Climate Crisis arises in response to the growing problem of climate change, driven both by the importance of disseminating information and raising awareness among the Venezuelan population of the effects of this planetary crisis, and by the need to build concrete actions to address this crisis. Accordingly, the main objective of the Plan is to increase understanding of climate change, its impacts and the actions needed to confront it, empowering communities to become agents of change. Through educational initiatives, awareness-raising campaigns and citizen participation programs, it seeks to encourage the adoption of adaptation and mitigation measures at the individual and collective level, promoting sustainable practices in various sectors and strengthening community resilience. Through an awareness-raising process at the community level, house by house, the Venezuelan population is informed about the impacts of climate change and offered practical tools that enable them to adapt to and mitigate its effects, demonstrating how small individual actions can generate a significant collective impact and contribute to building a more sustainable future.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: The Venezuelan population in general, prioritizing vulnerable communities and sectors at risk.

Users: The Venezuelan population in general, MINEC, Mayors' Offices, Governorates.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Promote Ecosocialist Committees at the national level, generating organizational structures for the promotion of climate crisis mitigation and adaptation actions, such as reforestation, collection of usable material and ecosocialist training programs throughout the country, training the population to face environmental challenges and build a more sustainable future.

4 | Value proposition

  • Increase the formation of Ecosocialist Committees.
  • Promote community participation in environmental, management and conservation issues.
  • Organize communities to achieve their socio-environmental empowerment.
  • Raise awareness and consciousness among the People's Power regarding the Climate Crisis.
  • Guide the implementation of climate change adaptation and mitigation measures from the local level.
  • Encourage the formation of ecologist, environmentalist and ecosocialist movements.

5 | Adaptation options

Through awareness-raising sessions on the climate crisis, community participation is promoted in collaboration with the Ministry of People's Power for Ecosocialism (MINEC) and its affiliated entities. This seeks to strengthen communities, raise awareness of the climate crisis and provide training on related topics, thereby driving local action to address environmental challenges.

6 | Key activities

  • Encourage the adoption of plants by the community for subsequent planting.
  • Promote the capture and collection of usable material.
  • Formation and adaptation of Ecosocialist Committees.
  • Recruitment of new Brigade Members against Climate Change.
  • Recruitment of Little Park Rangers.
  • Construction of Community Risk Maps.
  • Training and recreational activities related to the climate crisis, Receipt and handling of environmental complaints.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The National Awareness-Raising Plan against the Climate Crisis constitutes a social option and an enabling measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

The creation of Ecosocialist Committees, promoted by MINEC, is a key strategy to address environmental challenges in 647 prioritized communities. These committees focus on training and raising awareness of the population on environmental issues. Their main benefits include environmental education to reduce waste and promote recycling, adaptation to and mitigation of the climate crisis, and the fostering of ecological awareness to reduce the carbon footprint. The Ministry has assumed commitments such as the creation of community nurseries, training, the establishment of brigades against climate change, Technical Committees on Recycling and Cleaning, and the provision of weather stations and sorting bins. In each community, the aim is to build collective strategies for learning and preparedness for adverse events, prioritizing teamwork and training to improve the environment and quality of life.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Number of communal circuits served.
  • Number of communities served nationwide.
  • Number of homes visited nationwide.
  • Number of families reached nationwide.
  • Number of people sensitized nationwide.

Targets (2025-2030)

  • Establish 2.500 Ecosocialist Committees nationwide.
  • Sensitize 2.000.000 people annually on adaptation and mitigation against the climate crisis. (10.000.000 by 2030).

10 | Key actors

MINEO and its affiliated entities, Community Leaders, Spokespersons of Communal Councils and the organized community.

A22. PROMOTION OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION AND THE FIGHT AGAINST CLIMATE CHANGE

Sector: Ecosocialist Training

Context analysis

1 Problem definition

In recent years the highest temperatures on record have been reported; the climate crisis is intensifying and with it its effects on natural and social systems. The measures to be taken both to reduce global warming and to increase resilience to its effects depend largely on the degree of awareness and consciousness of society in general. Hence the importance of designing and implementing activities and publications that disseminate the role of the different actors in mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and what the people must do to increase resilience in the face of the onslaught of this crisis.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries: Students and teachers, the general population.

Users: Students and Teachers, the General Population, MPPE, MPPEU, MINEC, Mayors' Offices, Governorates.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Strengthen the development and promotion of environmental education for climate change adaptation, through various training activities, educational and outreach campaigns, and the production and publication of environmental texts of various kinds (specialized texts, guides, manuals, children's literature, among others), thereby stimulating environmental awareness in children, young people and adults, encouraging behaviors that promote environmental protection and environmentally friendly activities, and forming citizens who are aware of the current climate crisis and of the actions that can be taken, individually and collectively, to mitigate and adapt to climate change.

4 | Value proposition

Develop training and awareness-raising activities, as well as the production, publication and dissemination of environmental texts for children, young people, adults, students, professionals and the People's Power, addressing topics such as pollution, recycling, loss of biological diversity, the climate crisis, the protection of nature, clean energy, environmental culture, among other environmental aspects essential for strengthening the ecosocialist vision.

5 | Adaptation options

  • Training activities on environmental education and the fight against climate change.
  • Production and publication of environmental and climate change-related texts and literature.

6 | Key activities

  • Implementation of training activities (videoconferences, Forum-chats, Workshops, among others)
  • Implementation of educational and outreach campaigns in virtual mode.
  • Production and publication of specialized texts, children's literature, guides, manuals, among other learning and teaching resources.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The promotion of environmental education and the fight against climate change constitutes a social option and an enabling measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • Greater access by the entire population to teaching and learning resources related to environmental education.
  • Increase in the number of citizens sensitized to environmental conservation and climate change adaptation.

9 | Key metrics Indicators:

  • Number of texts published in print and digital media.
  • Number of people reached
  • Number of training and awareness-raising activities carried out Targets (2025-2030):

  • 4.000 training and awareness-raising activities carried out
