Gender Sector

A23. GENDER AND SOCIAL INCLUSION ACTION PLAN FOR CLIMATE CHANGE ADAPTATION IN THE AGRICULTURE, FISHERIES AND WATER RESOURCES SECTORS.

Sector: Gender

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

With the approval of the Bolivarian Constitution of Venezuela (1999), the State has intensified and deepened significant progress toward the objective of consolidating gender equality and equity, establishing a new social, participatory and democratic order that has undoubtedly opened important spaces for the visibility of women, leading to the strengthening of institutions for gender equality in Venezuela. A robust legal and institutional framework demonstrates the commitment of the Venezuelan State to take all necessary measures to ensure the elimination and eradication of discrimination against women, in favor of the institutional materialization of the social struggles of women in Venezuela, which had begun to take shape with the Equality Law. Therefore, it is expected that gender equality and non-discrimination in areas and communities vulnerable to climate change will remain a cross-cutting theme in the design and implementation of climate change adaptation actions within the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) to Climate Change in the Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources sectors.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: Women and girls in areas vulnerable to climate change, in the Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources sectors.

Users: Women and girls in areas vulnerable to climate change, MINEC, MinMujer, MPPATP, MINPESCA, MINAGUAS, People's Power, Governorates and Mayors' Offices.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Incorporate the gender and social inclusion approach and the elements of participatory strategic planning as guiding principles for decision-making and actions associated with the National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change in the Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources sectors.

4 | Value proposition

  • Consider the gender approach in the prioritization of adaptation actions, through the identification of gender-specific knowledge and capacities that can contribute to the planning and implementation of adaptation actions.
  • Carry out the recognition of actions that promote gender equality as co-benefits, for example, actions that recognize and empower women as agents of adaptation and strengthen the contributions that women are currently making to adaptation. Identifying specific adaptation options for women, men and marginalized groups according to their vulnerabilities and capacities, taking into account socially acceptable roles and responsibilities.
  • Design tracking indicators disaggregated by gender, to evaluate the effectiveness of incorporating the gender approach during the planning and implementation of the climate change adaptation process.

5 | Adaptation options

Gender and Social Inclusion Action Plan for Climate Change Adaptation.

6 | Key activities

  • Implementation of 39 participatory workshops to determine the needs and expectations of the People's Power in the design of the NAP.
  • Integrate the gender and social inclusion perspective into the vulnerability analyses of the agriculture, fisheries and water resources sectors.
  • Integrate the gender and social inclusion perspective into the process of identifying and formulating adaptation measures for the agriculture, fisheries and water resources sectors.
  • Integrate the gender and social inclusion perspective during the process of design, validation and follow-up of the NAP.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The Gender and Social Inclusion Action Plan for Climate Change Adaptation in the Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources sectors is considered a social option and an enabling measure for climate change adaptation.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • Guarantee the incorporation of gender analysis in the formulation, implementation and evaluation of the proposed National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change in the Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources sectors.
  • Ensure that the needs and priorities of women and vulnerable groups are considered in the design of the National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change in the Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources sectors.
  • Create internal structures and systems that promote gender equality and guarantee the equitable participation of women and men in decision-making linked to the design of the National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change in the Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources sectors.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Number of participatory workshops with the People's Power for the design of the NAP.
  • Number of women attending the participatory workshops with the People's Power for the design of the NAP.
  • Number of documents integrating the gender and social inclusion perspective in the design of the NAP.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • 39 participatory workshops with the People's Power for the design of the NAP.
  • 1248 women attend the participatory workshops with the People's Power for the design of the NAP.
  • 03 documents integrating the gender and social inclusion perspective in the design of the NAP.

10 | Key actors

MINEC, MPPATP, MINPESCA, MINAGUAS, MinMujer and Women Producers and Fishers.

Fisheries and Aquaculture Sector

A25. ASSESSMENT OF OCEANOGRAPHIC ENVIRONMENTAL VARIABLES IN THE TERRITORIAL SEA LINKED TO THE CLIMATE CRISIS

Sector: Fisheries and aquaculture

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

Evidence of changes in the historical trends of oceanographic variables in the territorial sea, such as sea temperature and primary productivity, which can directly affect fishery resources and activities.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: Fishing communities that benefit from a more balanced ecosystem in terms of populations of key species (to be restocked), Artisanal aquaculture producers who will benefit from training and aquaculture production manuals, and Other related post-capture and post-harvest actors: cold-storage operators, processing plants, national retail outlets, exporters.

Users: Institutions for aquaculture management, planning and promotion (users of the information) and the Venezuelan population (food security).

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Assessment of oceanographic environmental variables in the territorial sea in times of climate crisis, using remote sensing information from 1981 (sea surface temperature -SST- and winds) and 1998 (chlorophyll a) up to 2025. This initiative began in 2024, and an estimated scope of 2 years with own resources is projected, after which a methodology for periodic updating of the database and thematic products will be established for permanent monitoring of the territorial sea. If financing is obtained, the scope of the assessments can be expanded with the consolidation of the “Fisheries, Aquaculture and Oceanographic Data Science Laboratory” project as a space for permanent observation and analysis of environmental, coastal, oceanographic, demographic and production information; and field validation of the oceanographic variables, as well as the capture of other environmental and biological variables to be correlated in the medium and long term.

4 | Value proposition

Improve knowledge of the current effects of the climate crisis on variables that influence Venezuelan marine ecosystems and fishery resources, as well as of the trends in these changes, in order to improve understanding of the current and future scenario and the capacity to generate adaptation proposals.

5 | Adaptation options

  • Analysis of variations and trends in sea surface temperature, winds and chlorophyll a, to obtain historical records from 1981 and 1998 to the present. With additional resources, field validation can be carried out to increase the accuracy of the observations.
  • Assessment of the most vulnerable fishery resources according to the climate scenarios analyzed.
  • Dissemination of results to raise awareness among fishing communities regarding the territorial changes observed and the potential effects on their livelihoods.

6 | Key activities

  • Development of time series for the assessment of sea surface temperature, wind and chlorophyll a in the territorial sea: capture,
  • Downloading, preparation and processing of the information
  • Generation of thematic products; drafting of reports with discussions and results.
  • Training activities for CENIPA technical staff.
  • Working meetings.
  • Outreach activities (academic community, fishing communities and the general public).

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The assessment of oceanographic environmental variables in the territorial sea is considered a social adaptation option and an enabling measure aimed at reducing the sector's vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • Greater understanding of the current environmental scenario of the territorial sea and possible future scenarios.
  • Foundations for the development of assessments relating the aforementioned variables to the most vulnerable fishery resources.
  • Material for dissemination in communities

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Number of progress reports produced.
  • Number of thematic products of historical assessment results.
  • Number of oceanographic variables assessed.
  • Number of working meetings.
  • Number of training activities for research staff.
  • Number of workshops in communities.
  • Number of written publications for dissemination.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • 6 progress reports produced.
  • 3 thematic products of historical assessment results.
  • 3 oceanographic variables assessed.
  • 6 working meetings.
  • 3 training activities for research staff.
  • 10 workshops in communities.
  • 2 written publications for dissemination.

10 | Key actors

MINPESCA (INSOPESCA, CENIPA, FONPESCA), MINEC, Communities of fishing interest for documentation and subsequent use of this information in intervention designs.

88.000,00 US$.

A26. STRENGTHENING AQUACULTURE FOR COMMERCIAL AND RESTOCKING PURPOSES

Sector: Fisheries and aquaculture

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

Aquaculture in Venezuela is a key source of employment, food and development for many communities. In 2021, shrimp production exceeded 50.000 tonnes, generating more than 500 million dollars in exports. In addition, mariculture has advanced with the cultivation of mollusks and macroalgae in the country. However, a significant number of families dependent on artisanal aquaculture face technical and economic challenges; therefore, strengthening the production of species such as coporo, cachama and trout with more sustainable methods, together with restocking programs for key fishery resources, is essential to ensure a resilient and prosperous future for the sector.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: Fishing communities that benefit from a more balanced ecosystem in terms of populations of key species (to be restocked). Artisanal aquaculture producers who will benefit from training and aquaculture production manuals, and Other related post-capture and post-harvest actors: cold-storage operators, processing plants, national retail outlets, exporters.

Users: Institutions for aquaculture management, planning and promotion (users of the information) and the Venezuelan population (food security).

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Strengthening of aquaculture for commercial and restocking purposes to increase the resilience of the fisheries and aquaculture sector.

4 | Value proposition

  • Scientific validation of inland fish farming systems with methods that reduce the consumption of commercial balanced feed, for the development of farming protocols and manuals.
  • Training in artisanal aquaculture methods with low investment costs and greater sustainability, as an alternative for food production and livelihoods in rural communities.
  • Such is the case of coporo, promoted by MINPESCA through the “Coporo Plan”, under an extensive production scheme with low balanced feed requirements (use of natural and symbiotic fertilization).
  • Restocking in the natural environment of species of ecological and/or fishing interest.
  • Strengthening of captive breeding packages for marine species of interest.

5 | Adaptation options

  • Fish farming technology packages that are more sustainable from an ecological and economic perspective.
  • Training and certification in alternative fish production methods.
  • Farming packages for species not dependent on balanced feed.
  • Restocking of aquatic species of interest.

6 | Key activities

  • Research activities: field trips, community diagnostics, maintenance and fertilization of ponds, breeding, feeding and rearing trials of species, weight gain determinations.
  • Data analysis and presentation of results.
  • Restocking sessions in the natural environment.
  • Training workshops for producers.
  • Development of farming manuals.
  • Dissemination of results (academic and fishing communities and the general public).

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

Strengthening aquaculture for commercial and restocking purposes is considered both a social and an institutional adaptation option and an enabling measure aimed at reducing the sector's vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • A strengthened, more sustainable and competitive artisanal aquaculture sector.
  • Greater sustainability of populations of species targeted by fisheries.

Indicators:

Targets (2025-2030):

A27. PRODUCTION OF BIOSALT THROUGH CO2 CAPTURE IN COASTAL COMMUNES WITH THE CULTIVATION OF BATIS MARITIMA

Sector: Fisheries and aquaculture

Context analysis

1 Problem definition

Saline bioagriculture with the cultivation of halophytic plants (salt-tolerant species) is a revolutionary strategy to combat the effects of climate change. These plants, adapted to saline environments, which can be harvested several times throughout the year, not only make it possible to use resources considered marginal (salinized soils and seawater), but "blue carbon" ecosystems also capture and store up to 10 times more carbon than tropical rainforests, restore ecosystems and produce ecological and sustainable food and economies.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries: Fishing communities (fishers, unloaders, artisanal processors, families) and other related post-capture actors: cold-storage operators, processing plants, national retail outlets, exporters.

Users: the Venezuelan population in general (food security)

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

With saline bioagriculture, up to 10 times more carbon can be captured and stored than in tropical rainforests per square meter of land. Therefore, making use of coastal areas lacking vegetation to encourage this crop is a pertinent measure.

4 | Value proposition

  • Assess coastal zones with potential for cultivating halophyte species.
  • Review and update proposed management criteria and regulations in coastal zones.

5 | Adaptation options

Improve resource management in coastal zones to increase their resilience to the effects of the global climate crisis, through the cultivation of a species that protects the soil and at the same time has productive potential.

6 | Key activities

  • Assessment of areas suitable for cultivation with Batis maritima.
  • Conducting pilot tests for cultivation.
  • Harvesting and processing of Batis maritima.
  • Evaluation of the yield and quality results of the product obtained
  • Dissemination of results (in fishing communities and to the general public).

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures The sustainable management of non-conventional natural goods is considered both a social and an institutional adaptation option and an enabling measure aimed at reducing the sector's vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • Knowledge of the cultivation process of Batis maritima and its processing to obtain biosalt.
  • Coastal populations participating in innovative local production processes with a species that is sustainable over time.

9 | Key metrics Indicators:

  • Area cultivated in coastal zones per year.
  • Amount of biomass collected per year.
  • Technical staff trained per year
  • Communities involved per year.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • 200 hectares cultivated
  • 2.000 tonnes of biosalt processed.
  • 200 people trained per year.
  • 14 communes involved per year.

10 | Key actors

MINEC, MINPESCA (INSOPESCA, CENIPA, FONPESCA), MINEC, Security forces and active participation of communities in the stages of restocking and monitoring of species.

A28. SUSTAINABLE MANAGEMENT OF STRATEGIC FISHERY RESOURCES

Sector: Fisheries and aquaculture

Context analysis

1 Problem definition

The combined effects of the climate crisis and direct anthropogenic pressures on fishery resources pose a very current challenge for sustainable fisheries management. In the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, there is a need to update regulations for the use of species under a special administration regime (such as sardine, octopus, lobster, shrimp, blue crab, billfish and tuna), as well as to incorporate new management criteria.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries: Fishing communities (fishers, unloaders, artisanal processors, families) and other related post-capture actors: cold-storage operators, processing plants, national retail outlets, exporters.

Users: Management and planning institutions (users of the information) and the Venezuelan population in general (food security)

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Achieve sustainable management of strategic fishery resources, by updating management criteria and policies with current scientific evidence.

4 | Value proposition

  • Updated assessments of fishery resources and fisheries, with emphasis on the following resources: sardine, octopus, lobster, shrimp, blue crab, billfish and tuna.
  • Proposals to update fisheries management criteria and regulations for the resources assessed and to be assessed.

5 | Adaptation options

Improve the fisheries management of these resources to increase their resilience to the effects of the global climate crisis, through the updating of management criteria and policies based on current scientific information.

6 | Key activities

  • Fisheries assessments: field trips, application of surveys, processing of biological samples and data processing.
  • Drafting of reports.
  • Working meetings
  • Inter-institutional discussions of results for updating policies and regulations.
  • Dissemination of results (academic and fishing communities and the general public).

Governance for adaptation

  • Populations of strategic species of fishing interest that are more sustainable over time.

Peoples: Wayuú / Añú Antonio Diaz Municipality of Delta Amacuro State. People: Warao Users: Indigenous peoples and communities, MPPPI, MINEC, Mayors' Offices and Governorates.

Carry out fundamental actions based on the ancestral knowledge and wisdom of the indigenous peoples and communities of the ancestral territories of Venezuela, on measures for adaptation to climate change and variability, valuing indigenous worldview, uses, customs and cultural practices and climate change science.

4 | Value proposition

Indigenous peoples have developed strategies for adapting to climate change over the centuries. Their ancestral knowledge, practices and worldviews are key to the fight against climate change. Water Resources Sector

A30. POPULAR WATER MANAGEMENT

Sector: Water Resources

Context analysis

1 Problem definition

Decreases in precipitation rates and increases in temperature severely affect the hydrological cycle, resulting in the occurrence of extreme phenomena related to droughts, overflows and floods that endanger the livelihoods of the population and the population in general. Likewise, water quality is affected by climate change, since rising temperatures reduce dissolved oxygen and with it the resource's capacity for self-purification; accordingly, there will be negative effects on morbidity rates related to waterborne diseases, and changes would also be expected in freshwater ecosystems and their associated diversity.

At the national level, the most significant effects of decreased precipitation and increased temperature are expected in the regions where the population of the states of Miranda, Falcón, Trujillo, Táchira, Distrito Capital, Portuguesa, Nueva Esparta, Sucre, Guárico and Amazonas is located, in terms of the reduction of water sources due to the effects of droughts and sea level rise in coastal areas.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: The population using water resources in Miranda, Falcón, Táchira, Distrito Capital, Guárico and Amazonas.

Users: Water resource users, MinAguas, Hidroven, Water utilities and Territorial Water Service Units (UTAA).

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Strengthening of People's Power bodies for the comprehensive management of water, seeking to reduce vulnerability to the effects of climate change, achieving a greater response by the population to events that may affect the national water system, and the responsible use of water resources.

4 | Value proposition

The protection of the national water system through the training of spokespersons throughout the national territory will make it possible to reduce the vulnerability of communities and their livelihoods to climate change. This proposal is aimed at communities organized as People's Power, integrates Public servants as working People in Water Management, and addresses the vulnerabilities of the national water system through the following methodologies: Participatory Action Research, Socio-natural Risk Management, Environmental Education and Education for Sustainable Development.

5 | Adaptation options

Awareness-raising and training programs for participants in Water Management that enable adaptation to the impacts of Climate Change in coordination with communal government bodies (Water Technical Committees, Community Water Councils and Community Water Management Rooms) in the states of Miranda, Falcón, Trujillo, Táchira, Distrito Capital, Portuguesa, Nueva Esparta, Sucre, Guárico and Amazonas, applying as adaptation measures the Production and Propagation of plant species for water protection (nurseries); Structural and Agronomic Measures for watershed conservation; Reuse of wastewater and Use of surface water to diversify supply sources.

6 | Key activities - Strengthening of Communal Organization for Water Management in the states of Miranda, Falcón, Trujillo, Táchira, Distrito Capital, Portuguesa, Nueva Esparta, Sucre, Guárico and Amazonas. - Implement a Training Program for participants in Water Management in these states, with the following topics: Water Sowing and Harvesting; Production and Propagation of plant species for water protection (nurseries); Structural and Agronomic Measures for watershed conservation; Reuse of wastewater and Use of surface water to diversify supply sources. - Follow-up, control and evaluation.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

Popular water management is considered both a social option an enabling measure aimed at fostering awareness of climate risks and vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits Direct benefits:

  • Protection of the water system. strengthening of the People's Power Water Brigades (BRIPPA) and the Water Protection and Safeguarding Brigades (BRIPRA).
  • Protection of communities. Co-benefits:
  • Environmental: conservation of watersheds and biological diversity.
  • Sociocultural: conservation of cultural expressions linked to water resources.
  • Economic: Agricultural production, conservation of water flow that will maintain the hydroelectric power service

9 | Key metrics Indicators:

  • Number of communal organizations for water management strengthened.
  • Number of training workshops for popular water management.
  • Number of participants in the training program for participants in popular water management. Targets (2025-2030):
  • 06 training workshops for popular water management, per year.
  • 360 participants in the water management training program, per year.

10 | Key actors

MINAGUAS, Hidroven, Territorial Water Service Units, Governorates, Mayors' Offices, Communal Government as an expression of the Democratic Culture of water-related services, Water Technical Committees, Communal Councils, Communes.

A31. WATER USE MANAGEMENT IN COMMUNITIES

Sector: Water Resources

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The decrease in precipitation and the increase in atmospheric temperature have affected the supply cycles of the drinking water service, affecting some hydrographic regions, such as those assessed within this first group, which is made up of the states of Nueva Esparta, Sucre, Falcon, Portuguesa and Guárico.

The phenomenon of global climate change has had unbalancing effects on ecosystems and has made it necessary to implement management plans that adapt to these changes. Water, as a natural resource that is essential, vital and irreplaceable for life, has been affected in its production in some areas, where climate change has reduced the magnitude of its contribution through changes in rainfall events in terms of duration, intensity and frequency. As a consequence, new sources have been tapped in order to provide the service.

The planned actions contribute to improving the service by reusing wastewater and diversifying natural sources with improvements within the ecosystem.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries: The population using water resources in Nueva Esparta, Sucre, Falcón, Portuguesa and Guárico.

Users: Water resource users, MinAguas, Hidroven, Water utilities and Territorial Water Service Units (UTAA).

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Water Use Management in Communities for the Collection, Treatment and Reuse of Wastewater, relieving the aqueduct system and optimizing consumption through the rational, optimal and sustainable use of water in all its uses, reducing vulnerability to the impact of climate change.

4 | Value proposition

  • Select alternatives that include the reuse of wastewater; this makes communities less vulnerable to the action of climate change
  • Help reduce the consumption of drinking water in activities that do not require it, relieving the aqueduct system and optimizing consumption according to the quantity and quality of water.
  • Carry out Use Management in Communities for the Collection, Treatment and Reuse of Wastewater.

5 | Adaptation options

Management of the Reuse of Wastewater, through its Collection and Treatment, for domestic hygiene activities, in the states of Nueva Esparta, Sucre, Falcon, Portuguesa and Guárico.

6 | Key activities - Use of the resource in Communities through Reuse after the treatment of Wastewater. - Demand will be minimized and the resource will be put to its own use, where members of vulnerable communities affected by the effects of climate change will benefit from the implementation of a system consisting of a Flow Separator Box, which compactly incorporates the WWTP process, consisting of: 1. Physical Process:

  • Screening
  • Grease trap
  • Settling tank. 2. Biological Process:
  • Biodigester (Anaerobic Treatment). 3. Chemical Process (which will depend on the values yielded by the Water characterizations with respect to BOD OR COD): Chlorination System. With this type of infrastructure, the Final Disposal of the resource to the receiving stream is guaranteed, as well as the reuse of Wastewater, generating a notable contribution and minimizing the use of drinking water for irrigation and gardens. - Raise community awareness on the use of the Service. - Train Staff for the stewardship of Service Management.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures Use Management in Communities is considered both a structural option and an implementing measure aimed at guaranteeing the supply of drinking water to communities and thereby reducing vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits Direct benefits Optimizes consumption, relieving the aqueduct system, and reduces the consumption of drinking water in activities that do not require it.

Co-Benefits Integrative management model, which will make it possible to obtain favorable results with the rational, optimal and sustainable use of water in all its uses, with the participation of the popular government.

9 | Key metrics Indicators:

  • Water resource production (LPS).
  • Water resource demand (LPS).
  • Number of areas supplied. Targets (2025-2030):
  • 5 pilot systems for the Collection, Treatment and Reuse of Wastewater.

MINAGUAS, Hidroven, Territorial Water Service Units, Governorates, Mayors' Offices, Communal Government as an expression of the Democratic Culture of water-related services, Water Technical Committees, Communal Councils and Communes.

A33. IMPLEMENTATION OF EARLY WARNING SYSTEMS (EWS) IN PRIORITIZED RESERVOIRS TO REDUCE VULNERABILITY TO THE EFFECTS OF CLIMATE CHANGE

Sector: Water Resources

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

In the country, water systems were designed with a return period based on historical hydroclimatic data that, at the time, did not consider potential changes related to climate variation. In recent years such variation has intensified, increasing the vulnerability of water sources such as rivers, aquifers and reservoirs, by directly impacting the water balance. Reservoirs are among the most vulnerable hydraulic works. In Venezuela, reservoirs supply water to 70% of the population and are crucial for food and energy production; this situation is critical. Such climate variability calls for the implementation of Early Warning Systems (EWS) and the strengthening of climate information, both to generate an evidence base for designing adaptation solutions that achieve maximum impact and for the design and implementation of predictive models, in order to reduce the vulnerability of the population and their property.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries: The general population with regard to drinking water and electricity services, at local, regional and national levels, farmers and livestock producers.

Users: Communities near the reservoirs, farmers and livestock producers, water utilities (Hidrológicas), MPPAT, MINPESCA, MINEC, MPPEE.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Reduction of vulnerability to climate change variability and its effects on reservoirs, to avoid floods affecting the population or shortages of water resources intended for human consumption, food production and electricity production.

4 | Value proposition

  • Strengthen the governance and participation of communities to ensure the protection and conservation of reservoirs and their protective zones.
  • Strengthen the capacities of the population and raise awareness of the impacts of climate change.
  • Consolidate the safety of dams and reservoirs to ensure the availability of water resources for the various uses.
  • Increase efficiency in the use of water resources to ensure availability for the various uses.

5 | Adaptation options

With 82 operational reservoirs, EWS implementation is prioritized for 28 reservoirs, which have a high impact at the local, regional or national level, considering as relevant aspects, in strict order: the resource for human consumption, food production from the country's large irrigation systems, and electricity generation as an important part of this sector. In addition, consideration is given to the high response speed of their storage basin to variability in precipitation or temperature, which leads to rapid variation in storage levels.

The 28 prioritized reservoirs are: Aragua: Camatagua, Taiguaiguay, Suata; Miranda: Quebrada Seca, Lagartijo, Taguaza; Carabobo: Pao Cachinche, Canoabo; Cojedes: Pao La Balsa; Lara: Dos Cerritos, Atarigua, El Ermitaño; Zulia: Burro Negro, Tres Ríos, Manuelote, Tule; Falcón: El Iriso, Hueque, Barrancas, Maticora; Sucre: Turimiquire; Anzoátegui: Vista Alegre, Guacamayal, Boca De Uchire; Guárico: Tierra Blanca, Tamanaco, Tiznados, El Cigarrón; Portuguesa: Boconó Tucupido; Yaracuy: Cumaripa, Monagas: El Guamo; Barinas: Masparro; Mérida: Onia.

6 | Key activities - Coordination among institutions for the installation of EWS equipment and instruments at each reservoir, as well as activities to prepare facilities or operational areas for the organization of the different actors. - Hiring of professionals for capacity building. - Hiring of professionals for the design or updating of Risk Management Plans for each reservoir. - Contracting for the acquisition and installation services of EWS equipment and instruments. - Daily monitoring of availability and control of withdrawals from the reservoirs.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The implementation of Early Warning Systems (EWS) in prioritized reservoirs to reduce vulnerability to the effects of Climate Change is considered both a social option and a direct measure for reducing climate risks and vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

At the national level, optimal storage is ensured to meet demands for human consumption, irrigation and electricity generation. Also, increased efficiency in water management in the reservoirs, and protection of communities near the reservoirs against floods. In addition, jobs will be created, and improvements made in the technology for operating the reservoirs.

A34. STRATEGIC ACTION PROGRAM (SAP) FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF THE TRANSBOUNDARY WATER RESOURCES OF THE AMAZON RIVER BASIN, CONSIDERING CLIMATE VARIABILITY AND CHANGE

Sector: Water Resources

Context analysis

11 Problem definition Venezuela is linked to the project through the Casiquiare - Río Negro Basin, which has an area of 53.801,12 km , representing 5,87% of the country's total, located in Amazonas state, specifically in the municipalities of Maroa and Río Negro. Hydrographically it forms part of the Hydrographic Region identified as 12 “Amazonas”, which covers a total of 179.321 km and, specifically, in Venezuela's reports linked to Indicator 6.5.2. of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) on Transboundary Basin Management, it is identified as the Amazon River Basin / Casiquiare - Río Negro Sub-basin (Hydrographic Unit 484, according to the Pfafstetter method). It therefore requires ensuring the Integrated and Sustainable Management of the Transboundary Water Resources of the Amazon River Basin, considering climate variability and change.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries: Directly, the indigenous groups and inhabitants of the population centers distributed in the Casiquiare - Río Negro basin, amounting to 4.329 inhabitants, of whom 2.302 are men and 2.027 women. Users: Communal councils, fishers, agricultural producers, indigenous organizations and communities, tourism service providers, mayoralties and the government of Amazonas state, Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO), Ministry of Ecosocialism (MINEC), INPARQUES, MPPRIJP, MPPRE, MINAGUAS, MINTUR, MinDefensa.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision The Implementation of the Strategic Action Program (SAP) to ensure the Integrated and Sustainable Management of the Transboundary Water Resources of the Amazon River Basin considering Climate Variability and Change aims to strengthen the institutional framework for the coordinated and coherent planning and execution of activities for the protection and sustained management of the water resources of the Amazon Basin in the face of the effects of climate change experienced in the Basin. In addition, it seeks to achieve a shared vision for the sustained development of the region, based on the protection and integrated management of transboundary water resources, as well as adaptation to climate change.

4 | Value proposition

  • Strengthen institutional capacities in Integrated Water Resources and Environmental Management processes.
  • Promote Climate-Smart Agricultural Practices for the livelihoods of rural communities exposed to extreme events (floods and massive sediment transport) through the implementation of an early warning system.
  • Development of nature-based measures to minimize the effect of floods and recovery of terrestrial ecosystems in the Casiquiare - Río Negro Basin, Amazonas state (Venezuela).
  • Monitoring of water quality and vulnerable aquatic ecosystems, for the sustainable management of prioritized hydrobiological resources in the Casiquiare - Río Negro Basin, Amazonas state.

5 | Adaptation options The Ministry of People's Power for Ecosocialism (MINEC) as National Environmental Authority and Coordinator of Watershed Conservation processes, through the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO) and the implementation of the Strategic Action Program (SAP), leading to a process of adaptation of the population settled in the Casiquiare river - Río Negro basin, as well as promoting transdisciplinary and collaborative processes and work with key institutions such as MINEC -MINAGUAS-INAMEH.

6 | Key activities

  • Institutional strengthening of water governance at the regional (ACTO) and national (each country) levels.
  • Strengthened communities and ecosystems, capable of adapting to extreme hydrological events.
  • Compatible information across the basin to inform political decision-making in

IWRM and for the conservation of aquatic ecosystems.

  • Long-term sustainability of IWRM, offering socioeconomic and environmental benefits from

the effective implementation of the SAP at the national and regional levels.

  • Better understanding of the transboundary environmental impacts of large infrastructure projects.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures The Strategic Action Program (SAP) to ensure the Integrated and Sustainable Management of the Transboundary Water Resources of the Amazon River Basin, considering climate variability and change, is considered a direct institutional (implementing) option to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

Among the benefits, the following can be highlighted: - Increased institutional integration and training of the Amazonian countries in regional monitoring and management of water resources. - Decision-making capacity based on the availability of information at the regional level. - Standardization of procedures and parameters for water quality monitoring and installed capacities (laboratories, equipment). - The Project is executed within the framework of four components: i) Innovative governance model for Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) in the Amazon Basin (from the community to cabinet-level government); ii) Building community resilience and ecosystem protection against the effects of climate change; ¡ii) Integrated environmental monitoring and reporting in support of IWRM in the Amazon basin and iv) Comprehensive information system to monitor the progress of overall SAP implementation.

9 | Key metrics (2025-2030)

  • Survey of the hydrometeorological information baseline.
  • Installation, monitoring and maintenance of Hydrometeorological and hydrometric measurement stations in the Casiquiare-Río Negro river basin that contribute to the data managed by the National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMEH), the Amazon Regional Observatory (ARO) and the National Observatory for the Climate Crisis (ONCC).
  • Establishment of Climate-Smart Agricultural Practices (PACI).
  • Conduct training on Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN).
  • Sampling and assessment of degraded soils in the areas determined by the LDN methodology.
  • Identification of local practices used to minimize soil and land degradation (among other products of hydroclimatic events).
  • Identification and implementation of a group of Nature-based Solutions (NbS) alternatives to minimize the effects of soil degradation.
  • Strengthen the capacities of the key actors involved for the analysis of the soil situation corresponding to SDG 15, Target 15.3, Indicator 15.3.1.
  • Establish a soil sampling and assessment system that contributes to the data managed by the Amazon Regional Observatory (ARO) and the National Observatory for the Climate Crisis (ONCC).
  • Design and launch a group of sustainable agricultural practice (SAP) alternatives, using nature-based solutions (NbS) to support the maintenance of food production, adding the associated costs.
  • Formulation of a baseline that makes it possible to identify sampling points in the Casiquiare river - Río Negro basin.
  • Identify the areas to be monitored (300 km of aquatic ecosystems) on the basis of comprehensive and permanent monitoring of aquatic ecosystems in the Casiquiare river - Río Negro basin.
  • Characterization of surface water quality in the basin.
  • Define the prioritized monitoring indicators and hydrometeorological parameters, in identified and vulnerable areas and compatible with the data managed by the Amazon Regional Observatory (ARO) and the National Observatory for the Climate Crisis (ONCC).

A35. CONSERVATION AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT OF THE LAKE MARACAIBO BASIN

Sector: Water Resources

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

Eutrophication and hypoxia in Lake Maracaibo, caused by excess pollutants and nutrients from agro-productive activities, domestic wastewater discharges and industrial effluents without adequate treatment in the coastal zone, have intensified the environmental degradation of the basin and the loss of environmental benefits. In this context, the Venezuelan State is promoting the project Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Lake Maracaibo Basin as a contribution to the improvement of the large marine ecosystem of the Caribbean Sea.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries:

Direct beneficiaries: indigenous communities, fishers' councils, agricultural and livestock producers, local and national authorities, government institutions, environmental NGOs, universities and research centers, local population in vulnerable areas (particularly in the South of the Lake region).

Indirect beneficiaries: population living in the Lake Maracaibo basin

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision Address eutrophication and hypoxia in Lake Maracaibo by reducing the flow of nutrients and pollutants from agro-productive activities and untreated wastewater discharges, to contribute to the socio-environmental sustainability of the basin and the increase of the environmental benefits of the Caribbean Large Marine Ecosystem. This climate action also contributes to the mitigation of GHG emissions in the INGEI sectors: Waste (Wastewater treatment), Agriculture (management of agricultural soils) and LULUCF (Forest land, cropland, Wetlands, settlements).

4 | Value proposition

  • Strengthens institutional and community capacities for informed decision-making in the integrated management of the Lake Maracaibo Basin (CLM).
  • Strengthens the public policy framework to incentivize and finance actions that mitigate the problems of eutrophication and hypoxia in Lake Maracaibo.
  • Implements innovative models and practices to mitigate pollution in the CLM, strengthening livelihoods and food security.

5 | Adaptation options

  • Early warning systems (EWS) for harmful algal blooms; agroclimatic risk EWS; flood and high-water risk EWS.
  • Land Use Planning and Regulation Plans (PORU) for the Chama and Escalante river sub-basins, incorporating guidelines for the implementation of ecosystem-based solutions applied in production systems, nutrient management and integrated pest management.
  • Environmental sanitation plan for the CLM with emphasis on nutrient reduction and the rehabilitation and management of WWTPs.
  • financial instruments to promote the adoption of ecosystem-based solutions in production systems in the South of the Lake region.
  • Community local savings and credit system with a gender and intercultural approach implemented to promote resilience and sustainable production.
  • Action plan for the sustainable management of mangrove forests.
  • Action plan for sustainable soil management in agricultural production areas in the south of Lake Maracaibo.
  • Implementation of pilot tests for sustainable agricultural production.

6 | Key activities

  • Definition of thresholds for early warning
  • Training workshops for the establishment of agroclimatic technical working groups.
  • Calculation of hydrographic and hydrodynamic models of the hydrographic units of the CLM, including climate change and variability scenarios.
  • Design, preparation and publication on the project platform of bulletins disseminating information on agroclimatic risks, harmful algal blooms, and high water and floods in the CLM.
  • Diagnosis of existing conditions for the application of financial instruments that promote the adoption of ecosystem-based solutions applied in production systems, taking into account previous experiences.
  • Diagnosis and analysis of the biophysical and socioeconomic components (including the situation of indigenous peoples and communities) in the Chama and Escalante river sub-basins.
  • Definition of objectives and targets for nutrient reduction and infrastructure improvement (rehabilitation and expansion of WWTPs).
  • Investment planning considering cost estimates, sources of financing and investment schedule.
  • Execution of full-scale pilot projects for agricultural, urban and indigenous community areas incorporating ecosystem-based solutions for nutrient removal.
  • Preparation of a technical document on pilot plan experiences and their incorporation into the proposed Basin Sanitation Plan.
  • Initial assessment for the sustainable mangrove management pilot project.
  • Monitoring and Evaluation of sustainable mangrove management pilot interventions and proposed Action Plan for the improved management of mangrove forests.
  • Implementation of sustainable soil management pilot interventions.
  • Monitoring and Evaluation of sustainable soil management pilot interventions and proposed Action Plans.
  • Identification of good agricultural practices according to the different socio-environmental contexts of the basin.
  • Implementation of the global Soil Doctors programme.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The Project Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Lake Maracaibo Basin as a contribution to the improvement of the large marine ecosystem of the Caribbean Sea is considered a direct institutional option with the People's Power (implementing); it establishes ecosystem-based Adaptation and mitigation solutions to reduce vulnerability to climate change and contribute to the reduction of GHG emissions.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • Reduced vulnerability of communities and agricultural producers to extreme climate events and harmful algal blooms.
  • Availability of financial instruments for sustainable and resilient agricultural production.
  • Availability of planning instruments for sustainable agricultural production and watershed conservation.
  • Availability of instruments for sustainable soil management in agricultural production areas with pilot tests implemented. Co-benefits:
  • Strengthening of food security, reduction of losses in the agricultural sector.
  • Strengthening of food security, increased income for small agricultural producers.
  • Communities with sustainable and resilient agricultural production practices.
  • Strengthening of food security, increased income for small agricultural producers.

9 | Key metrics (2025-2030)

  • Number of Early Warning Systems (EWS) designed and linked to the environmental risk management subsystem.
  • Number of agroclimatic technical working groups (MTA) in operation representing the upper, middle and lower basin in the CLM.
  • Number of hydrographic units of the CLM with hydrological, high water and flood, and hydrodynamic models, including climate change and variability scenarios.
  • Number of participatory diagnostic workshops held with key actors for the formulation of proposals for financial instruments to promote the adoption of ecosystem-based solutions in production systems
  • Number of community savings and credit organizations established with a gender and intercultural approach.
  • Number of sub-basins that have an environmental sanitation plan that includes an investment plan for the rehabilitation of infrastructure and for increasing treatment capacity
  • Number of pilot tests implemented in agricultural areas, urban centers and indigenous communities as a complement to plant treatment for nutrient removal
  • Number of sustainable management pilot tests of mangroves and agricultural areas implemented with local actors as part of the execution of action plans.
  • Number of people trained as promoters in the Soil Doctor Programme.
  • Number of communities of practice established implementing sustainable soil and mangrove management pilot tests.
  • Number of cocoa and coffee biotrade pilot projects implemented in the South of Lake Maracaibo region.

Key actors from the public and private sector (ICLAM, MINEC, MINAGUAS, HIDROLAGO, MAT, State Governments, Mayoralties, Producer associations, local communities, agroclimatic working groups and People's Power.

Risk Sector

A36. EARLY WARNING SYSTEM FOR THE UPPER AND MIDDLE BASIN OF THE MANZANARES RIVER IN SUCRE STATE

Sector: Risks

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

85 % of the national population is located in the Coastal and Andes mountain ranges, with a very high population density that turns natural habitats into urban landscapes, generating habitat loss and fragmentation and negatively impacting the provision of ecosystem services by watersheds. Climate variability and climate change are modifying the natural patterns of meteorological phenomena, affecting these areas with greater frequency of occurrence and intensity; the decrease in forest cover in the upper basins, land-use change and inadequate soil management lead to an increase in the areas at hydrometeorological risk; as has occurred over the last 10 years in the Andes, in the basins of the Mocotíes (in Mérida) and Boconó (in Trujillo) rivers; in the Central Coastal mountain range, in the basins of the Petaquire-Mamo river and the La Zorra stream in La Guaira, the Chorrerón-Los Patos stream in Tejerías, Aragua state, and in the Eastern mountain range, the Manzanares river in Sucre state. This problem makes it necessary to consider updating the Land Use Planning Plans and designing Local Adaptation Plans for these regions, which make it possible to identify the areas with the greatest vulnerability due to surfaces exposed to adverse hydrometeorological events, and to implement Early Warning Systems (EWS) in them as part of the adaptation measures. To this end, the EWS monitor would be of great strategic value in the middle and upper basin of the Manzanares river in Sucre state, as it lies within the Turimiquire Massif protective zone, which covers part of the states of Anzoátegui, Sucre and Monagas, where the Turimiquire reservoir, the main source of water supply for Margarita Island, is also located.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries: The Early Warning System (EWS) will benefit vulnerable communities, allowing them to act in advance, ensuring inclusion in evacuation plans, generating tools for leadership and active participation in risk management, and promoting cooperation and support between communities and the institutions that exercise governance. The EWS will also directly benefit biological diversity and the agro-productive and commercial sectors operating within the municipalities located in the middle and upper basin of the Manzanares river.

Users: Mayoralties, State Government, Civil Protection, Fire Departments, CORPOELEC, MINAGUAS, MINEC, INAMEH and the general population.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision The Early Warning System for Adverse Hydrometeorological Events will seek to generate and disseminate warning information in a timely and meaningful manner, in order to enable the communities of Cumanacoa, La Fragua and Las Trincheras, settled in the upper and middle basin of the Manzanares river, to be prepared to act appropriately and with sufficient advance time to reduce the possibility of major losses or damage from severe weather events that may occur, in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, in its article 55, and in the National Risk Plan, as well as in the Organic Law of the Homeland Plan of the 7 Great Transformations 2025-2031 (G.O. N° 6907, 24/05/25), considering that reducing the risk from the impact of floods and mass movements means guaranteeing ecosystem services in a watershed.

4 | Value proposition

  • Determine the needs, vulnerabilities and organization of the communities living within the upper and middle basin of the Manzanares river.
  • Survey and characterization of the basin in terms of hazard, vulnerability and risk, through participatory situational analysis by the community.
  • Installation and operation of the network of automatic stations.
  • Training of the community for the construction, operation and maintenance of community rain gauges and level gauges for the community observation network.
  • Operation of the Early Warning System, recording and real-time transmission of data from both the network of automatic stations and the community observation network.
  • Design of the Emergency and Warning Dissemination Plan.
  • Evaluation and adaptation of the Community Early Warning System.

5 | Adaptation options

INAMEH will provide short-, medium- and long-term weather and climate forecasts for users' decision-making in case of risk from floods and mass movements, regarding ecosystems and land uses in the watersheds; these provide ecosystem services to communities, the construction of sustainable civil works for sediment control and channelization of riverbeds, water production in the different seasons of the year to meet the water demand of vegetation and crops, and provide water availability in reservoirs for supply and irrigation purposes and other water bodies, thus maintaining biological diversity in general.

6 | Key activities Year 2025

  • Train communities on community-based early warning systems together with INAMEH.
  • Define vulnerable areas based on the community's primary knowledge.
  • Characterize, through a hydrogeomorphological study, the middle and upper basin of the Manzanares river, with its spatial distribution of areas vulnerable to floods and mass movements.
  • Define measurement points in the middle and upper basin of the Manzanares river. Year 2026
  • Install 3 automatic climate stations plus the staff gauges.
  • Train the community in the operation and construction of community rain gauges and staff gauges.
  • Calibrate the watershed to adjust the parameters of a hydrological model and estimate thresholds.
  • Validate the siting of the station network.
  • Keep the automatic weather stations in optimal condition. Years 2027 - 2028
  • Train the population on methods for disseminating alarms and uploading data generated by the community rain gauge network.
  • Validate the rainfall-runoff models and adjust precipitation and level thresholds.
  • Keep the automatic weather stations in optimal condition. Years 2029 - 2030
  • Verify thresholds for the EWS.
  • Train the community on evacuation drills in response to a warning and sustainability plans for extreme hydrometeorological events.
  • Keep the automatic weather stations in optimal condition.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The Early Warning System for the upper and middle basin of the Manzanares river in Sucre state is considered a social option involving community-based adaptation and an implementing measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

Community Early Warning Systems (EWS) contribute to the safety, sustainability and resilience of communities in the face of floods and landslides, generating broad benefits:

  • Economically and environmentally, EWS directly benefit biological diversity and planning in the agro-productive sectors, allow measures to be implemented to minimize damage to infrastructure and services, contribute to safe urban planning with sustainable construction and land-use practices, and promote the integration of technologies.
  • From a social point of view: they significantly reduce mortality from these events, guaranteeing the most vulnerable communities access to information and assistance, promoting equity and gender equality in disaster preparedness, increasing trust between the community and governance with a more efficient response; they promote a culture of prevention and risk management in the community, create a sense of belonging and mitigate population displacement.

9 | Key metrics Indicators:

  • Number of maps submitted.
  • Number of intensity/duration/frequency (IDF) curves.
  • Number of reports submitted.
  • Number of calendars submitted.
  • Number of tables submitted. Targets (2025-2030):
  • 1 map of the watershed with the location of the weather stations.
  • 2 intensity/duration/frequency (IDF) curves for the watershed.
  • 1 report with the analysis of flows and levels of the Manzanares river and tributaries according to historical availability.
  • 1 map of accessibility, hazards and vulnerability.
  • 1 seasonal calendar.
  • 1 table of precipitation and level thresholds.
  • 1 land use map.
  • 4 training workshops for the community and governance.
  • 1 summary report with the structured interviews.
  • 1 inventory of community leaders.
  • 1 updated manual for the construction, installation and data collection of community rain gauges and staff gauges.
  • 1 operating manual for the mobile application for uploading rain gauge and staff gauge data.
  • 1 community hydrometeorological community risk map.

National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMEH), Vice Ministry of Risk Management and Civil Protection (Operational Zones for Damage Assessment and Needs Analysis), ZOEDAN Sucre, Ministry of People's Power for Ecosocialism (MINEC), Civil Protection, Fire Departments, Mayoralties, State Government, Communal Councils, general population, Water Technical Working Groups.

A37. PLAN FOR DROUGHT EVENTS FOR THE UPPER BASINS OF THE GUÁRICO, TIZNADOS, ORITUCO, TAMANACO AND UÑARE RIVERS IN GUÁRICO STATE

Sector: Risks

Context analysis

11 Problem definition

The dry climates of the upper watersheds of the Guárico, Tiznados, Orituco, Tamanaco and Uñare rivers in Guárico state are considered highly vulnerable to drought events, which affect land preparation, planning of the sowing calendar, and water demand in all its spheres; they are prone to an increase in forest fires caused by inadequate management, putting the land at risk of degradation and even desertification; currently such risk shows a tendency to manifest itself and worsen in the immediate future due to climate change and climate variability.

2 | Beneficiaries and users

Beneficiaries: The population located geographically within these basins. Agricultural producers and biological diversity in general.

Users: Mayoralties, State Government, Civil Protection, Fire Departments, CORPOELEC, MINAGUAS, MINEC and INAMEH.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

The Plan for Drought Events will seek to be a key public policy management tool, at the municipal and state levels, whereby the community, agricultural producers, and the municipal and state governance sectors operating in the geographical areas where the upper basins of the Guárico, Tiznados, Orituco, Tamanaco and Uñare rivers of Guárico state are located will be able to be informed about drought threats and the risk of forest fire spread, led by INAMEH, through meteorological and climate forecasting based on the network of community and automatic stations, enabling the application of the preventive, mitigating and corrective measures established in the National Risk Plan, the National Drought Plan, as well as in the Organic Law of the Homeland Plan of the 7 Great Transformations 2025-2031 (G.O. N° 6907, 24/05/25), considering that reducing the risk from the impact of floods and mass movements means guaranteeing ecosystem services in a watershed.

4 | Value proposition

  • Determine the degrees of hazard and vulnerability to drought and the incidence of forest fires.
  • Delimit the land uses that have been exposed to droughts and forest fires.
  • Train the members of the working groups to be formed with environmental management modules.
  • Develop management indicators for the key metrics.
  • Apply the early warning system for drought.
  • Execute the plan for drought events.

5 | Adaptation options

INAMEH will provide short-, medium- and long-term weather and climate forecasts for users' decision-making in case of risk of droughts and forest fires, regarding the ecosystems and land uses located in the watersheds; these provide ecosystem services to communities, such as water production in the different seasons of the year, add soil moisture required for the water demand of vegetation and crops, and provide water availability in reservoirs for supply and irrigation purposes and other water bodies, thus maintaining biodiversity in general.

6 | Key activities Year 2025 - Estimate the spatial distribution of drought and forest fires in the upper watersheds selected above. - Carry out a spatial characterization of the exposed surfaces vulnerable to droughts and forest fires. - Prepare a baseline study based on the risk to the rural population. Year 2026 1. Hold comprehensive training workshops aimed at work teams committed to participating, leading with the community, agricultural producers and the governance sectors. Years 2027-2030 - Analyze environmental indicators for monitoring strategies for the integrated management of drought and forest fires. - Apply the national and regional drought plan as direct support to the national risk and climate change adaptation plans. - Validate the degree of effectiveness of the execution of the Plan for Drought Events initiated in 2025.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The Plan for Drought Events for the upper basins of the Guárico, Tiznados, Orituco, Tamanaco and Uñare rivers in Guárico state is considered an institutional option and an implementing measure to reduce vulnerability to climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

The Plan for Drought Events will provide benefits and co-benefits to the entire study area:

  • From an environmental and economic point of view: it will be a key public policy management instrument for municipal and state governance in the risk sector, agricultural producers and the community in general, by providing vital climate information for taking strategic measures in the agricultural sector, in the integrated management of water resources, in the control of vegetation fires and in the sustainable and sustained availability of the ecosystem services offered by these basins, actions that are considered within the national-level drought and climate change adaptation plans (to be published), which seek to reduce impacts and increase resilience.
  • From a social point of view, it will contribute to reducing the risk of internal rural-urban migration, poverty, and to gender equity, increasing the social well-being of the community.

9 | Key metrics Indicators:

  • Number of maps submitted.
  • Number of reports submitted.
  • Number of plans designed. Targets (2025-2030):
  • 60 monthly maps of meteorological drought indices.
  • 12 monthly maps of the hydrological drought index (SDC).
  • 48 reports with weekly meteorological and climate forecasts for the region.
  • 182 daily maps forecasting the risk of forest fire spread (December to May).
  • 1 land use map.
  • 5 drought risk vulnerability maps for each year.
  • 5 maps validating the behavior of drought risk in the region for each year.
  • 5 maps validating the behavior of forest fire risk in the region for each year.
  • 1 plan for drought events.

10 | Key actors

National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMEH), Vice Ministry of Risk Management and Civil Protection (Operational Zones for Damage Assessment and Needs Analysis), ZOEDAN Guárico, Ministry of People's Power for Ecosocialism (MINEC), General Directorate of Ecosystem Management and Conservation Policies - Directorate of Soil Conservation, Desertification and Drought, Civil Protection, Fire Departments, Mayoralties, State Government, Communal Councils, general population and Association of Agricultural and Livestock Producers.

Health Sector

A38. ENTOMOLOGICAL SURVEILLANCE AND VECTOR CONTROL

Sector: Health

Context analysis

1 Problem definition

Climate change represents a risk to human health, due to the increase in environmental health factors (physical, chemical and biological); for example: heavy rainfall and floods, and increases in temperature and relative humidity, favor the emergence of vectors and reservoirs of parasites or viruses that cause metaxenic diseases, the contamination of water supply sources, affecting their quality, greenhouse gas emissions, among others.

The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela is highly vulnerable to the incidence of diseases produced by vectors that are sensitive to climate alterations, because it is located in the tropical zone; in view of this situation, the State maintains cutting-edge policies adhering to the principles and methods of the Pan American Health Organization/World Health Organization (PAHO/WHO), based on Integrated Vector Management, where local knowledge, risk micro-stratification, intersectorality and community participation converge in the management of metaxenic disease prevention programs.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries:

The general population, with special attention to people living in areas vulnerable to climate change. Users:

MINEC, MPPS, the general population, taking into consideration vulnerable people such as children, older adults, pregnant women and, in particular, attention to people living in areas of high and very high vulnerability to climate change.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Strengthen entomological surveillance and vector control, also including health surveillance and control of water quality and of air quality at stationary sources (incinerators) at the national level in the face of climate change.

4 | Value proposition

  • Carry out monitoring of the number and type of diseases associated with climate change that are controlled or eradicated.
  • Strengthening of basic response capacities in entomological surveillance and vector control of diseases associated with climate change.

5 | Adaptation options

  • Entomological risk assessment and impact on vector control in the face of climate change.
  • Risk and impact assessment on water quality control in the face of climate change.

6 | Key activities

  • Train professional and technical health personnel, the ASIC, organized communities and governmental and non-governmental organizations in entomological surveillance actions and vector control measures within the framework of integrated vector control management at the national level in the face of climate change.
  • Strengthen basic response capacities in entomological surveillance and vector control within the framework of integrated vector control management at the national level in the face of climate change, by updating the methodological framework, supplying materials and inputs, ecological characterization and correlation of environmental variables (temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, among others) and supervision of surveillance and control activities.
  • Strengthening of sanitary surveillance and control of supply systems (water sources, treatment and distribution system) and water quality monitoring in the face of climate change.
  • Train professional and technical health personnel, the ASIC, organized communities and governmental and non-governmental organizations in surveillance actions and climate-resilient drinking water safety plans at the national level.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

Entomological surveillance and vector control related to climate change is considered a social information option for monitoring the effects of climate change.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits

  • Strengthening of integrated vector and disease control management at the national level in the face of climate change by updating the methodological framework.
  • Strengthening of sanitary surveillance and control of water and air quality at the national level in the face of climate change.

9 | Key metrics

Indicators:

  • Number of personnel trained (professional and technical health staff).
  • Number of awareness campaigns carried out in communities.
  • Number of diseases controlled or eradicated. Targets (2025-2030):
  • Train and educate at least 200 professional and technical public servants in the health sector.
  • Reach at least 100 vulnerable communities through awareness campaigns.
  • Reduce by at least 80% the risk factors associated with diseases generated by climate change.

10 | Key actors

MINEC, MPPS, Medical care centers, Universities and Research Centers related to the health field.

11 Budget and costs

555.000 US$

12 | Sources of financing (current or future)

Institutional financing.

Labor Sector

A39. PROMOTION OF A RESILIENT AND SUSTAINABLE WORK ENVIRONMENT

Sector: Labor

Context analysis

1 Problem definition

Identifying problems in adapting to climate change in the labor sector is essential to promote work environments that are safe, sustainable and prepared to face present and future climate change challenges. Climate change is one of the greatest global threats affecting various sectors, including labor. Variations in climate, such as rising temperatures, extreme weather events and changes in resource availability, directly impact the productivity, health and safety of workers.

2 | Beneficiaries and users Beneficiaries: Workers (men and women), Work entities, Communities near the work entity.

Users: Local economy and the community in general.

Adaptation actions

3 | Adaptation vision

Promote a resilient and sustainable work environment that guarantees the safety and well-being of workers in the face of climate change, as well as the viability of work entities toward a safe and healthy environment.

4 | Value proposition

  • Implement training and awareness programs.
  • Promote healthy work practices.
  • Promote safe and healthy workspaces.
  • Establish performance and monitoring indicators.
  • Foster inter-institutional collaboration.

These specific objectives seek to foster a comprehensive framework that guarantees not only the safety and well-being of workers, but also the sustainability and viability of work entities, communities and various labor organizations with regard to climate change adaptation.

5 | Adaptation options

  • Inform and guide workers (men and women), employers (men and women), as well as labor organizations (unions, prevention delegates (men and women) and CPTT) about their participation and role in climate change adaptation, as multiplier agents in the social work process, their family and community environment.
  • Contribute to the training of leaders capable of promoting and facilitating processes of participation, organization, integration and consensus-building that result in activities in favor of climate change adaptation.
  • Implement participatory plans within workspaces, based on a satisfactory understanding of the processes, methods and techniques essential for carrying out the activities

6 | Key activities

  • Design and implement an awareness, information and guidance campaign for the workers (men and women) of the MPPPST and its affiliated entities on greenhouse gas emissions, nationally determined contributions (NDC) and climate change adaptation. This action aims to raise awareness among these economic entities of the great responsibility they must assume in the fight against climate change. It will be carried out through workshops, talks, videoconferences, among others.
  • Establish links of effective interaction between the sectors, the central, regional and local government and the communal level, to implement actions that contribute to the fight against climate change; this coordination will facilitate training and multiply experiences that have yielded results in this area.
  • Creation of a National Training Program (PNF) on climate change mitigation and adaptation for the labor sector.
  • Education and training: Promote the development of training and awareness programs to increase workers' preparedness for extreme climate events and promote a culture of prevention and action.
  • Develop an adaptation framework that enables workers and employers to face the challenges of climate change, guaranteeing health, safety and productivity in the workplace and its surroundings.
  • Holding of workshops and talks in order to raise awareness among the working
  • class and their surroundings regarding the importance we must give to Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation. Carrying out this action requires coordination with the Ministry of People's Power for Ecosocialism and its Ecosocialist Territorial Units.

7 | Type of adaptation options and measures

The promotion of a resilient and sustainable work environment is considered a social education option and an enabling measure for climate change adaptation.

Governance for adaptation

8 | Benefits and co-benefits a. Increased Job Training

  • Specific Knowledge: Workers acquire skills and knowledge on how to adapt to changing climate conditions, improving their response capacity.
  • Certifications: Possibility of obtaining training certifications on climate change topics (or define what type of certification) that increase employability and professional recognition. b. Increased Productivity
  • Effective Strategies: Implementation of work practices that optimize productivity, even under adverse climate conditions.
  • Reduction of Lost Days: Fewer workdays lost due to illness or extreme climate conditions. c. Improved Health and Safety
  • Safer Work Environments: Knowledge of safety measures that reduce climate-related risks.
  • Workers' Health: Reduction of climate-related illnesses and improvement of general well-being. Social benefits
  • Collective Adaptation: Foster a sense of community and collaboration between workers and employers to face climate challenges.
  • Social Solidarity: Promote social cohesion by involving various stakeholders in training, and implement measures at the community level in the face of vulnerability and latent risks. Environmental benefits
  • Environmental Awareness: Increased awareness of the importance of conservation and the responsible use of natural resources.
  • Sustainable Work Practices: Promotion of practices that minimize environmental impact, contributing to sustainability. Innovation and Development of New Technologies
  • Promotion of Innovation: Training that drives research and development of adaptive technologies.
  • Promotion of innovative solutions that can be implemented in the work environment.
  • Work entities that implement training plans are seen as responsible and committed to the well-being of their workers and the environment.

Implementing a training plan for climate change adaptation not only benefits workers and work entities at the individual level, but also generates co-benefits that positively impact the community, family

9 | Key metrics Indicators:

  • Number of community events or initiatives involving workers in climate change adaptation.
  • Number of workers trained in a culture of climate change adaptation.
  • Number of communities benefited
  • Number of work entities benefited with a resilient and sustainable work environment.
  • Number of partnerships formed between work entities, governments and non-governmental organizations to address climate change.

Targets (2025-2030):

  • Number of events held or participation in community initiatives involving workers (men and women) in climate change adaptation:112 community events and initiatives
  • Workers trained: 15% (2025-2027), 20% (2028-2030) Base population 3000 Workers (men and women) Work entities benefited with a resilient and sustainable work environment: 10% (2025-2027), 20% (2028-2030). Number of partnerships formed between work entities, governments and non-governmental organizations to address climate change.15 Partnerships

and the environment. This comprehensive strategy is essential for building a resilient and sustainable working future.

10 | Key actors

Ministry of People's Power for the Social Labor Process (MPPPST), Ministry of People's Power for Ecosocialism (MINEC), Ministry of People's Power for Communes, Social Movements and Urban Agriculture (MPComunas),
